body.text: High-voltage direct-current (HVDC) converter transformers are at the core of modern power transmission systems. As energy systems evolve and renewable integration increases, HVDC technology enables efficient long-distance transmission with reduced losses and enhanced controllability.
HVDC converter transformers act as the critical interface between the AC grid and HVDC systems, ensuring precise voltage adaptation and stable operation under complex electrical conditions.

Siemens Energy HVDC converter transformers combine decades of engineering expertise with advanced design and manufacturing capabilities to deliver high-performance solutions for ultra HVDC (UHVDC) applications (offshore and onshore). With a proven track record in major transmission projects, Siemens Energy supports reliable and efficient power transmission across diverse grid environments.
The importance of HVDC transformers in the energy transition
In the transition toward a more sustainable and interconnected energy system, HVDC transformers play a critical role in enabling reliable power transmission.
HVDC converter transformers are highly specialized high-voltage components used in converter stations, forming the critical interface between AC grids and HVDC transmission systems.

As a key component in UHVDC and long-distance transmission projects, HVDC transformers enable efficient AC/DC power conversion, supporting bulk power transmission at DC-voltage levels such as 800 kV and 1100 kV. This enables efficient long-distance power transmission with reduced losses, particularly for large-scale infrastructure projects.
HVDC converter transformer design ensures:

items: Precise voltage adaptation for converter systems
Reliable insulation between AC and DC systems
Reliable operation under combined AC/DC electrical stress

body.text: While the transformer itself does not perform the AC/DC conversion, it ensures stable converter operation and enables efficient, controllable and low-loss power transmission.
These capabilities make HVDC transformers a key enabler of modern power transmission systems and future-proof grid infrastructure.
How does an HVDC transformer work?
To understand this role in more detail, it is important to look at how an HVDC converter transformer operates within a converter station.
Within a converter station, the HVDC transformer operates in close coordination with power electronic converters (e.g. LCC or VSC systems) to enable efficient AC/DC power conversion.
Simplified process flow:

items: AC power enters the HVDC transformer from the grid
The transformer adjusts the voltage to match converter requirements
The conditioned power is transferred to the converter valves
The converter performs rectification (AC to DC) or inversion (DC to AC)

body.text: This process enables:

items: Controlled power flow
Stable grid integration
Efficient long-distance transmission with minimized losses

HVDC Classic vs HVDC Plus® technologies
HVDC converter transformers are used in both line-commutated converter (LCC) systems, commonly referred to as HVDC Classic, and voltage source converter (VSC) systems, known as HVDC Plus®.

While HVDC Classic is typically applied in large-scale, long-distance bulk power transmission projects, HVDC Plus® enables more flexible applications such as offshore wind integration, multi-terminal systems and dynamic grid stabilization.

As a result, HVDC converter transformers are specifically designed to meet the distinct electrical and operational requirements of each technology, ensuring reliable performance across a wide range of transmission scenarios.

As part of the HVDC converter station, HVDC converter transformers provide:

items: Voltage adaptation for rectifier and inverter operation
Electrical isolation between AC and DC systems
Reliable handling of UHVDC and power levels
Optimized efficiency to minimize transmission losses and reduce overall system operating costs

body.text: Their design must also withstand:

items: Combined AC/DC voltage stress
Harmonic distortion from converter operation
Dynamic load conditions

body.text: This makes HVDC converter transformers more complex than conventional high-voltage transformers, requiring advanced insulation, winding design and cooling solutions to ensure reliable operation and long-term performance.

faqs.q: What is a phase‑shifting transformer (PST)?
faqs.a: A phase‑shifting transformer (PST) is a sophisticated high‑voltage transformer designed to actively steer the direction and magnitude of power flows in AC transmission networks. It does so by injecting a variable voltage perpendicular to the line voltage. Thus a PST determines how much active power moves along a specific line — effectively turning it into a strategic tool for shaping load flows in highly meshed transmission systems.This capability allows operators to relieve overloaded corridors, balance parallel circuits, and maintain system stability even under rapidly changing operating conditions.

faqs.q: Why are PSTs becoming increasingly important as transmission grids evolve?
faqs.a: Modern transmission systems face rising complexity: cross‑border energy trading, fluctuating renewable generation, and the interplay of long‑distance transmission corridors all intensify the need for precise power‑flow management. PSTs offer exactly that. By redirecting power into desired paths, they: reduce congestion in critical grid sections,support more efficient use of existing infrastructure,help align physical flows with market‑driven schedules, andenhance operational security during disturbances or outages. Their robustness and controllability make PSTs a central element in strengthening grid resilience—especially in regions with dense interconnections and high transit flows.

faqs.q: How do PSTs contribute to the success of the energy transition?
faqs.a: The energy transition introduces strong regional generation patterns and highly variable feed‑in profiles, particularly from wind and solar. PSTs provide the flexibility transmission system operators need to keep the grid stable while integrating large shares of renewables. They enable: targeted routing of renewable electricity from production hubs to load centers,effective congestion management without immediate grid expansion,greater operational flexibility in hybrid AC networks, anda more resilient system architecture capable of handling dynamic power flows. In short, PSTs help ensure that the grid becomes smarter, stronger, and future‑ready—supporting a secure transformation toward a decarbonized energy system.

faqs.q: How do PSTs contribute to the success of the energy transition?
faqs.a: The main purpose of a phase shifting transformer is to manage active power flows within AC transmission networks. By adjusting the phase angle between two grid nodes, a PST helps redirect power flows to relieve congestion and support stable system operation.

faqs.q: Where are phase‑shifting transformers (PSTs) used?
faqs.a: Phase‑shifting transformers are installed in high‑ and extra‑high‑voltage transmission systems, particularly in meshed networks and parallel transmission corridors where power flow paths need to be actively managed.

faqs.q: What are the advantages of using a phase‑shifting transformer (PST)?
faqs.a: A PST enables targeted power flow control, improves use of existing grid capacity, and helps reduce congestion without grid expansion.

faqs.q: What are the limitations of a phase‑shifting transformer (PST)?
faqs.a: Phase‑shifting transformers are large, highly customized units that require detailed planning and system studies. Their impact is dependent on network topology, and they are primarily suited for steady‑state power flow control, not fast dynamic regulation.

faqs.q: How does a phase‑shifting transformer (PST) compare to alternative congestion management solutions?
faqs.a: Phase‑shifting transformers provide an effective solution for long‑term power flow control, particularly where grid constraints are structural. Other technologies may offer faster response, but often with increased complexity and higher lifecycle costs.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a conventional transformer and a phase‑shifting transformer (PST)?
faqs.a: While a conventional transformer adjusts voltage levels, a phase‑shifting transformer modifies the phase relationship between voltages, directly influencing active power flow in the transmission system.

faqs.q: Can a phase‑shifting transformer (PST) be used on a single-phase system?
faqs.a: For transmission applications, phase shifting transformers are designed for three phase systems to ensure symmetrical operation and controlled power flow. Single phase use is not common in practical grid applications.

Expert Insights: How phase shifting transformers optimize power flow and prevent grid overloads
Phase shifting transformers are essential for managing power flow in increasingly complex grids. Hear from experts how they work, why they matter, and what defines Siemens Energy's approach.
What is a phase‑shifting transformer (PST)?

A phase‑shifting transformer (PST) is a specialized high‑voltage power transformer designed to control active power flow in AC transmission networks. It allows grid operators to steer both the direction and magnitude of power flows on specific transmission lines without changing generation.

A PST achieves this by injecting a variable voltage component perpendicular to the line voltage, thereby adjusting the phase angle. This makes the phase‑shifting transformer a strategic tool for managing line loading, relieving overloaded corridors, and balancing parallel circuits in highly meshed transmission systems. As a result, system stability can be maintained even under rapidly changing operating conditions.
How PSTs work

Phase‑shifting transformers influence power flow by introducing a controllable phase‑angle shift between the sending and receiving ends of a transmission line. This is commonly achieved using an indirect PST design, which combines a shunt (or tap) unit with a series unit that injects a variable voltage into the line.

Depending on system requirements, PSTs can be designed as two‑core solutions, offering high operational flexibility for large power ratings, or as single‑core solutions up to 230 kV, typically selected where space, transport, or site constraints apply.
Why PSTs matter in today's smart grids

Transmission grids are increasingly shaped by renewable generation, meshed interconnections, and unplanned loop flows. As power follows physical laws rather than commercial schedules, congestion frequently occurs on critical transmission corridors.

Phase‑shifting transformers provide grid operators with a targeted and proven tool to manage these flows and maximize the efficiency of the existing grid. They support renewable integration, reduce redispatch measures, and help maintain system stability in highly interconnected AC networks.
Key customer challenges PSTs address
Unwanted power flows and loop flows

In meshed AC transmission networks, power flows are governed by network impedance rather than commercial schedules. This natural load distribution can lead to loop flows and unscheduled cross‑border power exchanges, where electricity takes unintended paths through neighboring systems.

Such conditions increase the risk of overloading individual transmission lines and can adversely affect adjacent grids. Phase‑shifting transformers enable grid operators to actively influence these flows, restoring controllability and predictability in highly interconnected transmission systems.
Limited transmission capacity and congestion

Rising electricity demand, renewable generation, and cross‑border trading place growing pressure on existing transmission infrastructure. In many regions, grid expansion is constrained by permitting, cost, or long lead times.

Phase‑shifting transformers help increase the usable transmission capacity of existing networks by shifting power flows toward underutilized corridors. This targeted flow control allows operators to relieve congestion and defer or avoid costly grid reinforcements, while maximizing the efficiency of installed assets.
Grid stability and security of supply

Secure grid operation requires maintaining stability under normal operation and contingency conditions. Events such as line outages or sudden changes in generation can quickly alter power flow patterns and challenge N‑1 security.

Phase‑shifting transformers support grid stability by enabling controlled power redistribution following disturbances. They contribute to improved system resilience, faster recovery after outages, and the secure reconnection of network elements in complex transmission grids.
Integrating renewables and cross‑border trading

The increasing share of renewable energy sources and the expansion of cross‑border electricity markets add variability and complexity to transmission system operation. Market coupling further intensifies power exchanges across national boundaries.

Phase‑shifting transformers act as an enabler for large‑scale renewable integration and cross‑border power trading. By providing precise control of active power flows, they support secure system operation while facilitating efficient and reliable market‑based electricity exchange.

Benefits of Siemens Energy phase‑shifting transformers
Operational and grid benefits

Phase‑shifting transformers provide active power flow control to optimize the loading of parallel transmission lines and network sections. By mitigating loop flows and reducing congestion, they improve asset utilization and restore controllability in meshed AC transmission networks. This enhanced flow control increases grid stability, operational flexibility, and system independence for transmission system operators and interconnectors.
Economic and strategic benefits

By making better use of existing infrastructure, phase‑shifting transformers help avoid or defer costly grid reinforcements. They increase usable transfer capacity on critical corridors, supporting higher trading volumes and revenue potential on interconnectors. In addition, optimized power flows contribute to lower system losses and improved overall network efficiency.
Sustainability and energy transition

Phase‑shifting transformers enable higher shares of renewable energy by directing power flows away from congested nodes and toward available transmission capacity. They support secure, efficient, and climate‑friendly transmission planning, helping grids adapt to increasing variability while advancing the energy transition.
Siemens Energy portfolio and technical capabilities
Design variants and ratings

Siemens Energy phase‑shifting transformers are available in single‑core and two‑core designs, with three‑phase execution and multiple configuration options to suit different grid topologies and site constraints. The selected design concept is driven by system requirements such as operational flexibility, space availability, transport limitations, and redundancy needs.

Phase‑shifting transformers are engineered for high‑voltage transmission applications, covering a wide range of voltage levels and power ratings. Typical solutions address transmission systems up to the highest voltage classes and very high-power ratings, with high phase‑shift capability, fine tap resolution, and a broad operating range to support precise power flow control under varying network conditions.
Key technical features

Siemens Energy phase‑shifting transformers combine compact mechanical design with options for low‑noise execution, ester insulation, and advanced cooling concepts, supporting both environmental and site‑specific requirements.

They are designed for high reliability and long‑term operation, featuring robust mechanical construction and compliance with international standards for transmission applications. Where required, phase‑shifting transformers can be equipped with digital monitoring and online diagnostics, supporting condition‑based maintenance and integration into modern substation automation environments.
Application configurations

Phase‑shifting transformers can be implemented in in‑line or by‑pass arrangements, depending on operational philosophy and network topology. These configurations allow targeted control of active power flows while maintaining flexibility for maintenance and contingency operation.

Typical applications include interconnectors between control areas, tie‑lines between transmission systems, and internal corridors affected by persistent congestion. In each case, PSTs provide grid operators with a controllable element to manage power flows in complex and highly interconnected AC transmission networks.
Siemens Energy's consultative approach
Grid studies and specification support

Siemens Energy supports transmission system operators with pre‑project grid studies to determine the required capabilities of a phase‑shifting transformer within the specific network context. Subject‑matter experts analyze system behavior, contingencies, and operating scenarios to translate grid challenges into clear technical requirements.

This process is carried out in close collaboration with customer network planners, ensuring that system needs, operational objectives, and regulatory constraints are reflected in technical specifications and tender documentation.
Co‑creation of cost‑optimized specifications

Key parameters such as power rating, phase‑shift range, short‑circuit levels, and tap changer configuration have a direct impact on both performance and cost. Siemens Energy applies an iterative, collaborative specification process to evaluate these trade‑offs transparently.

By combining engineering expertise with system knowledge from the customer side, specifications are refined to achieve a cost‑efficient, robust, and future‑proof solution aligned with long‑term grid development plans.
From design to energization

Siemens Energy provides end‑to‑end project support, covering engineering, manufacturing, testing, logistics, installation, and commissioning. This integrated approach ensures consistency from initial system studies through to energization on site.

With a global manufacturing footprint and extensive reference experience across multiple regions, Siemens Energy supports reliable project execution under diverse technical, environmental, and regulatory conditions.
Typical use cases and reference scenarios
Cross‑border interconnectors

Phase‑shifting transformers are widely applied on cross‑border interconnectors to control active power exchange between control areas. They help limit unscheduled flows, support market coupling, and protect neighboring transmission systems while maintaining secure operation.
Congested internal corridors

Within national or regional grids, PSTs are used on persistently congested internal corridors to redistribute power flows. By steering power toward underutilized paths, they relieve bottlenecks and maximize the efficiency of existing transmission infrastructure.
Renewable integration hubs

At locations with high concentrations of renewable generation, phase‑shifting transformers support the integration of variable power sources by directing flows away from congested nodes. This enables higher renewable penetration without compromising grid stability.
Blackout prevention and system restoration support

Phase‑shifting transformers contribute to system security and resilience by supporting controlled power flow during contingencies. They play a role in blackout prevention, post‑fault stabilization, and the safe reconnection of network sections during system restoration.
Service, lifecycle, and digital support
Service offerings

Siemens Energy supports phase‑shifting transformers throughout their lifecycle with preventive and corrective maintenance, spare parts management, and emergency support for installed PST fleets. Retrofit and upgrade options are available for aging assets, including tap‑changer modernization and condition‑monitoring enhancements.
Condition monitoring and diagnostics

Digital solutions such as online condition monitoring, data‑driven diagnostics, and asset health indices provide transparency on the condition of critical components. Where required, monitoring solutions can be integrated into asset management and substation automation systems for fleet‑wide visibility.
Training and operational support

Siemens Energy offers training for grid operators and maintenance personnel, supported by operational guidelines and assistance in defining operating philosophies. This helps ensure safe operation, optimized maintenance practices, and long‑term asset performance.

faqs.q: What is a power transformer?
faqs.a: A power transformer is a static electrical device that transfers energy between circuits at different voltage levels using electromagnetic induction. It plays a key role in AC power grids by enabling efficient transmission and distribution of electricity—from generation to consumption. Modern power transformers are designed to handle high electrical stress and often include on-load tap changers (OLTC) to regulate output voltage and maintain grid stability, which is increasingly important with the expansion of renewable energy sources.

faqs.q: What is the main function of a power transformer?
faqs.a: A power transformer’s main role is to convert voltage levels in the power grid—stepping up voltage for efficient long-distance transmission and stepping it down for safe local distribution. This process helps to minimize energy losses, ensure grid stability, and enable the integration of renewable energy sources. By adapting voltage to the needs of each grid segment, transformers are essential for a reliable and efficient energy supply.

faqs.q: How are Siemens Energy power transformers tested?
faqs.a: Each transformer undergoes rigorous factory acceptance testing (FAT), including routine, type, and special tests, to ensure compliance with international standards, customer requirements and reliable performance.

faqs.q: How much does a power transformer cost?
faqs.a: Costs depend on design complexity, specifications, and project requirements. Siemens Energy provides tailored solutions with transparent pricing upon request.

faqs.q: What causes a power transformer to fail?
faqs.a: Common causes include insulation breakdown, overheating, moisture, mechanical stress and mal operations. Siemens Energy mitigates these risks through design competence, digital monitoring and customer training.

faqs.q: What types of insulation fluids are used?
faqs.a: Siemens Energy transformers support mineral oil, natural and synthetic esters, and re-refined oils — selected based on performance, safety, and environmental criteria.

faqs.q: How do power transformers improve grid stability and efficiency?
faqs.a: They regulate voltage, balance loads, and reduce transmission losses , enabling stable, efficient, and resilient grid operation.

faqs.q: How do Siemens Energy transformers support the energy transition?
faqs.a: By enabling renewable integration, HVDC transmission, and digital grid management, Siemens Energy transformers play a key role in decarbonizing global energy systems.

faqs.q: What voltage and power ratings are available?

body.text: Siemens Energy's power transformers are essential building blocks of resilient and efficient power grids. Backed by decades of engineering excellence and a global manufacturing footprint, the transformers deliver reliable performance under the most demanding conditions. Each unit undergoes rigorous testing to meet the highest quality standards — ensuring long service life, grid stability, and operational efficiency. The comprehensive portfolio includes medium and large power transformers, supported by in-house R&D, digital innovation, and deep expertise in grid integration. From high-voltage transmission to renewable energy applications, Siemens Energy transformers enable the energy transition with proven technology and future-ready design.
Power transformer solutions for a changing energy landscape

As energy systems evolve toward decarbonization, decentralization, and digitalization, power transformers must meet increasingly complex demands. Siemens Energy offers tailored transformer solutions that support grid modernization, renewable integration, and cross-border energy exchange — all while ensuring reliability and efficiency.

Every Siemens Energy power transformer is a custom-engineered unit, designed and manufactured according to specific customer requirements. This bespoke approach ensures optimal performance, seamless grid integration, and long-term value across diverse applications.
Large power transformers

Siemens Energy's large power transformers are the backbone of high-capacity transmission and critical infrastructure projects worldwide. Engineered for maximum efficiency, durability, and grid stability, they ensure reliable energy flow across vast distances and complex networks. Whether reinforcing national grids or enabling intercontinental power corridors, each transformer is custom-designed to meet stringent technical and environmental standards, supporting the global energy transition.
Medium power transformers

Medium power transformers are built for flexible deployment in transmission and distribution networks, ensuring reliable performance across diverse applications. They are ideal for grid interconnections, industrial facilities, and renewable energy hubs. Each unit is custom-engineered, integrating features such as advanced cooling systems, eco-friendly insulation fluids, and digital monitoring for smarter operations.
Power transformer product types and applications

Siemens Energy offers a comprehensive portfolio of specialized power transformers, tailored to meet the evolving demands of modern grids. From load flow control and high-voltage direct current transmission to reactive power compensation, these solutions deliver efficiency, safety, and long-term reliability — even under the most challenging conditions.
Phase-shifting transformers

Phase-shifting transformers (PSTs) enable precise control of power flow in transmission networks. They help optimize grid utilization, reduce congestion, and facilitate cross-border energy exchange. Each PST is custom-built to regional requirements, ensuring seamless integration and operational excellence.
HVDC converter transformers

HVDC converter transformers are critical components in high-voltage direct current transmission systems. They enable efficient long-distance power transfer and support the integration of offshore wind farms and remote generation sites. Siemens Energy designs both HVDC Classic and HVDC Plus® transformers, tailored to specific converter technologies and system configurations.
Shunt- & series reactors

Shunt and series reactors cover the full spectrum of ratings and voltage levels requested worldwide, delivering solutions for every grid configuration and operational need. They help improve grid efficiency, reduce energy losses, and support dynamic network operations. Each reactor is engineered for reliability and tailored to meet the specific requirements of evolving power systems.
Mobile resilience transformers

Siemens Energy's mobile resilience transformers provide rapid-response solutions for grid emergencies, temporary substations, or disaster recovery.. Siemens Energy designs mobile units for fast deployment, ensuring reliable power supply during outages or infrastructure upgrades. These custom power transformers are engineered for flexibility, transportability, and high performance under time-critical conditions.

Innovative transformer technologies and features

Siemens Energy offers cutting-edge technologies as configurable options to meet the evolving demands of modern power systems. These innovations empower customers to enhance performance, enable digitalization, and support sustainability — making transformers future-ready and globally competitive, while driving the energy transition.

The Pretact® concept by Siemens Energy is designed to maximize the resilience of power grids through a modular system of preventive and protective features. It safeguards transformers and high-voltage equipment from operational disruptions, natural disasters, and unexpected outages. Additionally, highly adaptable plug-and-play mobile resilience units ensure rapid response during emergencies or scheduled maintenance—supporting a stable and uninterrupted power supply.

Siemens Energy's Pretact® Ecosafety is the world's first substation concept that integrates proven and newly developed technologies to elevate environmental protection, health, and safety. This innovative solution is designed to minimize the risk of fire and explosions, enhancing both resilience and sustainability. By reducing potential harm to nature and human life, Pretact® Ecosafety sets a new standard for safe and future-ready substations.

Siemens Energy is deeply committed to decarbonizing the energy sector and continuously advancing sustainability in both the supply chain and the core components of transformers. Through close collaboration with suppliers and customers, the company develops step-by-step solutions that reduce CO₂ emissions across the entire lifecycle. In parallel, Siemens Energy is actively working toward a circular economy, aiming to set new industry benchmarks for environmental responsibility and resource efficiency.

Power transformers are essential for the reliable transmission and distribution of electricity. Siemens Energy takes protection to the next level: with advanced materials and innovative designs, these transformers and reactors are not only resilient against extreme weather and grid fluctuations but also engineered to withstand ballistic attacks. This ensures the physical security of your assets and guarantees a stable, future-ready energy supply.
Flexible insulation fluids – tailored for sustainability, safety, and performance

Siemens Energy offers a versatile range of insulation fluids to meet diverse environmental and operational requirements. In addition to conventional mineral oil, natural esters, synthetic esters, and re-refined oils are provided. Each fluid type offers specific benefits depending on the application—such as improved fire safety, reduced environmental impact, or support for decarbonization goals. This flexibility allows transformer solutions to be customized for performance, sustainability, or regulatory compliance.

faqs.q: What is a shunt reactor?
faqs.a: A shunt reactor is an electrical device that absorbs excess reactive power to control voltage levels in AC transmission systems.

faqs.q: What is a series reactor?
faqs.a: A series reactor is a device installed in series with a circuit to limit current and control power flow by adding impedance.

faqs.q: What are fixed shunt reactors used for?
faqs.a: Fixed shunt reactors are used for constant reactive power compensation in stable grid conditions, such as long transmission lines.

faqs.q: When should variable shunt reactors be used?
faqs.a: Variable shunt reactors are used in dynamic grids with fluctuating load or renewable generation, where flexible compensation is required.

faqs.q: How do shunt reactors support renewable energy?
faqs.a: Shunt reactors stabilize voltage and manage fluctuations in renewable energy systems, especially in cable-based transmission networks.

faqs.q: Where are shunt reactors installed?
faqs.a: Shunt reactors are typically installed at line ends, busbars, or within substations in high-voltage transmission systems.

faqs.q: What voltage and power ratings are available?
faqs.a: Typical shunt reactors cover voltage levels from 33 kV to 800 kV and power ratings up to 300 MVAr.

body.text: In modern AC grids, maintaining voltage stability is becoming increasingly challenging as power flows become more dynamic. Shunt and series reactors are essential components for stable and efficient grid operation.

Shunt reactors are used to regulate reactive power and stabilize voltage, particularly under light-load conditions, while series reactors limit current and influence power flow by adding controlled impedance to transmission lines.

Siemens Energy provides shunt and series reactors as proven solutions for reliable and efficient grid operation. The portfolio ranges from 10 MVAr up to 300 MVAr and covers voltage levels from 25 kV to 800 kV—supporting demanding utility and renewable applications.

Depending on grid conditions, shunt reactors are available as fixed or variable solutions: fixed reactors support stable, predefined operation, while variable shunt reactors adapt dynamically to changing system requirements.
The following comparison illustrates how fixed and variable shunt reactors perform under different grid conditions.

body.text: Choosing the right solution depends on your grid dynamics.
Shunt reactors in modern power systems

In high-voltage AC systems, shunt reactors are used to regulate reactive power and support voltage control across transmission networks. They play a key role in mitigating overvoltage effects, particularly in long-distance transmission corridors and cable-based infrastructure.
Typical installation locations include:

items: At grid connection points along transmission corridors and cable links
Within substations, where centralized reactive power compensation is required
In high-voltage networks prone to voltage rise during light-load operation

body.text: Shunt reactors are particularly important under light-load or no-load conditions, where the capacitive behavior of transmission lines and cables can increase voltage levels and place additional stress on grid equipment.
Shunt reactor market
Customer needs

Power system operators are increasingly challenged to maintain voltage stability in transmission networks with long-distance AC links, extensive cable deployment, and fluctuating renewable generation. These conditions require reliable and efficient reactive power compensation, particularly under varying load scenarios.
Market trends

The shunt reactor market is shaped by grid reinforcement and the rapid expansion of cable-based infrastructure, including offshore and underground links. Key trends include higher efficiency designs, compact solutions for space-constrained installations, and the growing integration of digital monitoring for condition-based maintenance.
Market expectations

As grids continue to evolve toward higher complexity and variability, demand for shunt reactors is expected to remain strong. Utilities, representing the largest share of the market, are increasingly focusing on solutions that combine low losses, operational flexibility, and long-term reliability in dynamic grid environments.
Siemens Energy shunt reactor portfolio

Shunt reactors are essential for reactive power compensation and voltage control in high-voltage transmission networks. Depending on grid conditions, different reactor types provide the required level of stability, efficiency, and flexibility.
Siemens Energy covers the full range of reactor solutions for high-voltage transmission applications, supporting diverse grid requirements and customized system designs.
Fixed shunt reactors

Fixed shunt reactors provide constant reactive power compensation and are designed for stable, predefined grid conditions. They are widely used in high-voltage transmission networks, including long overhead lines and cable systems, where reliable voltage control and predictable operating conditions are essential.

As a proven and cost-efficient solution, fixed shunt reactors help maintain voltage stability, are used to regulate reactive power, and support reliable grid operation. They are particularly suited for applications with steady load profiles and limited variability.

In today's evolving energy systems, they continue to play a key role in ensuring stable transmission performance and are often deployed alongside power transformers to support efficient and secure grid operation.
Variable shunt reactors (VSR)

Variable shunt reactors (VSR) enable dynamic reactive power compensation by adjusting output to changing grid conditions. This makes them particularly suitable for modern transmission networks with fluctuating power flows.

They are widely used in renewable energy integration and cable-dominated grids, where generation and load conditions vary significantly. By continuously adapting compensation levels via tap changer technology, VSRs support voltage stability, improve efficiency, and reduce system losses.

As grid requirements evolve, VSRs provide the flexibility needed to maintain stable and reliable operation. Digital monitoring and predictive maintenance solutions further enhance performance, availability, and lifecycle efficiency.

The choice between fixed and variable shunt reactors depends on grid stability, load variability, and specific operational requirements. The following comparison provides a structured overview to support this decision.
Shunt reactor configurations
Shunt reactors are available in different configurations to meet specific system, installation, and operational requirements.
Single-phase and three-phase shunt reactors
Shunt reactors are available in single-phase and three-phase configurations, depending on system design and operational requirements.

Single-phase shunt reactors are typically used in specific transmission configurations or customized applications >= 550 kV. Three-phase shunt reactors are the standard solution for utility-scale grids <= 550kV.
Their balanced operation enables efficient integration into high-voltage transmission systems and supports reliable grid performance.
Oil immersed shunt reactors
Oil-immersed shunt reactors are widely used in high-voltage networks due to their strong insulation performance and efficient thermal management.
The insulating oil enables reliable operation under demanding electrical conditions while supporting long service life and stable performance over time.
These reactors are often combined with transformer service solutions to enhance long-term asset reliability and optimized lifecycle management.
Series reactors portfolio
Series reactors are connected in series with transmission lines or feeders, where they introduce controlled impedance to influence current flow and overall system behavior.

By increasing system reactance, they limit short-circuit currents to manageable levels and support the protection of critical grid equipment during fault conditions. This contributes to improved system stability and ensures reliable operation of transmission and distribution networks.

In addition, series reactors can support power flow control and help balance load between parallel lines. As part of modern grid solutions, they play an important role in enhancing system resilience and enabling stable operation under changing network conditions.
Shunt reactors applications and use cases
Shunt reactors are used across a wide range of applications, from substations to renewable energy systems, where stable voltage control is essential.
Shunt reactors in substations
In substations, shunt reactors stabilize voltage and manage reactive power, particularly in high-voltage transmission systems with varying load conditions.
Installed at busbars or line ends, they are used to regulate reactive power and voltage across the network, supporting reliable operation and efficient long-distance power transmission.
As substation designs evolve and system complexity increases, shunt reactors remain a key component for stable and reliable grid operation.
Utility-based shunt reactors

Utilities deploy shunt reactors as part of grid expansion, reinforcement, and modernization strategies. They support voltage control, reduce transmission losses, and improve overall system efficiency.

In large-scale transmission networks, shunt reactors help maintain power quality and ensure stable operation under varying load conditions. As grid infrastructures continue to evolve, they remain a key element in enabling reliable and efficient power delivery.
Renewable-based shunt reactors

Shunt reactors play a critical role in integrating renewable energy sources into modern power systems. They help manage voltage fluctuations and stabilize networks affected by variable generation from wind and solar power.
They also support compliance with grid codes by ensuring voltage stability and reliable operation in systems with high variability.

Typical applications include offshore wind connections, long HVAC cable systems, and hybrid renewable projects. These environments often require integration with digital grid solutions to manage increasing system complexity and maintain stable performance.
Key technical features and performance
Overview
The Siemens Energy portfolio covers a wide range of voltage and power ratings, typically ranging from 25 kV to 800 kV and from 10 MVAr up to 300 MVAr.
Key features include a compact and robust design, supporting reliable performance in high-voltage transmission environments.

Options for low-loss and low-noise operation are available. Variable shunt reactors can be specified with an extended regulation range (up to 80%) and sustainability-oriented design options, depending on project requirements.
Compact designs support space-constrained installations and can reduce substation footprint and overall infrastructure costs.
Together, these characteristics ensure high reliability, operational flexibility, and long service life across modern high-voltage transmission applications.
Comparison shunt vs. series reactor

In practice, shunt reactors are used to maintain voltage stability, particularly in long-distance transmission and cable-based systems. Series reactors, on the other hand, protect the grid by limiting fault currents and controlling load flow.
Together, both technologies contribute to a reliable, efficient, and resilient power system.
Benefits for customers
Siemens Energy reactors combine decades of engineering expertise with advanced design capabilities to support reliable and efficient grid operation.
From grid consulting and system design to manufacturing, testing, and lifecycle services, Siemens Energy supports customers across the entire project lifecycle.

Fixed shunt reactors are used for constant reactive power compensation in stable grid conditions, such as long transmission lines.
When should variable shunt reactors be used?
Variable shunt reactors are used in dynamic grids with fluctuating load or renewable generation, where flexible compensation is required.
How do shunt reactors support renewable energy?
Shunt reactors stabilize voltage and manage fluctuations in renewable energy systems, especially in cable-based transmission networks.
Where are shunt reactors installed?
Shunt reactors are typically installed at line ends, busbars, or within substations in high-voltage transmission systems.
What voltage and power ratings are available?
Typical shunt reactors cover voltage levels from 33 kV to 800 kV and power ratings up to 300 MVAr.

body.text: Compact, light and efficient

Siemens Energy develops and produces traction transformers for rolling stock applications of all relevant ratings and voltage levels. The focus is on maximum reliability, economic efficiency and safety – and ensuring that the transformers are perfectly in line with the customer's requirements.
Locations

Siemens Energy offers single-phase and multi-phase units in all capacity ranges up to 15 MVA and – upon customer request – even above. Units can be mounted in machine rooms, under-floor and low-floor applications, and for on-roof installation.
Ratings and voltages

Siemens Energy builds traction transformers with frequencies from 16 ⅔ to 60 Hz and rated power up to 15 MVA. Operating voltages include 1.5 kV DC, 3 kV DC, 12 kV, 15 kV, 25 kV as well as special voltage levels.
Cooling

Siemens Energy can design and customize the cooling unit to suit customer preferences, either integrated in the transformer in the full frame or as a separate component, entirely in accordance with the specific space requirements. Flexibility is also the order of the day when it comes to selecting cooling fluids. We have solutions for all capacity ranges that use oil, silicon, or an ester-based fluid (e.g. MIDEL 7131) that is very kind on the environment.
Windings and filters

For its traction transformers, Siemens Energy offers integrated smoothing and filter reactors; auxiliary and heating windings, depending on customer specifications; and traction windings as network filter reactors.
Leveraging data for maximum transformer performance

Siemens Energy transformers offer the opportunity to track the transformers in operation. Operators can not only monitor but optimize transformer performance. Monitoring and data analysis are the important factors for digitalization of traction transformer for rollingstock applications.
A new generation of sensors monitors transformer health

A modular multisensory system continuously monitors the “health” status of the transformer and modifies operation behavior according to the results of an onboard optimization algorithm. The Siemens Energy monitoring system leverages a new generation of sensors. These sensors transmit data to a local, remote or cloud-based control system. After data processing, the actors will – if necessary – receive commands for correcting the operation behavior.
Benefit from the performance data of other traction transformers

Economical and technical information of each traction transformer is updated online and collected to optimize all similar transformers in operation. Our real-time monitoring system optimizes cost of operation cost and maintenance intervals, increasing energy and economic efficiency.
Rely on Siemens Energy transformers – anywhere, anytime

Siemens Energy traction transformers operate a worldwide manufacturing and service network to serve customers all over the world. Our manufacturing sites worldwide adhere to European quality and sustainability standards – regardless of the manufacturing location.

body.text: Tests for maximum reliability and customer satisfaction

Siemens Energy uses the most advanced and comprehensive routine tests, type evaluations and special tests for maximized product reliability and customer satisfaction. Siemens Energy traction transformers are tested essentially in the same way as power transformers to ensure maximum safety and quality. Upon request, tests may be performed at an accredited third-party laboratory.

• Routine tests on each traction transformer acc. to EN 60310
• Type tests acc. to EN 60310
• Finite element method (FEM) of eigenfrequencies and stiffness
Investigation and special tests on request
• Shock and vibration test for traction transformer acc. to IEC 61373
• Short circuit test acc. to DIN EN/ IEC 60076-5
• Measurement noises acc. to EN 60076-10
• EMV investigation and special tests
Turning energy into speed

On-board Tractronic® traction transformers turn energy into speed that moves passengers and freight. As part of the traction chain, they are crucial to the performance of train and operator services. Siemens Energy designs and builds Tractronic® traction transformers in different specification profiles: Frequency, rating and voltage; Required dimensions and weights; Losses and impedance voltage characteristics; Operational cycles and frequency response behavior; Environmental requirements.

body.text: Decarbonization and sustainability goals can be achieved in many ways, and require different levels of investment and modification to existing plants and equipment. To help you achieve your goals, Siemens Energy offers reliable, well-proven solutions under six focus areas that can deliver significant impact but that require limited modification to existing assets.
Your Assets and Our Potential Solutions

Other Available Resources

AGT Decarbonization Brochure

Aggressive decarbonization goals and mandates require aeroderivative gas turbines to run on carbon-neutral and diverse fuels as soon as possible. Learn more about our range of decarbonization solutions and their impact.

Let Siemens Energy help you assess Hydrogen-based decarbonization infrastructure needs based on your impact targets.

Aeroderivative Gas Turbine Customer in Malaysia Achieves up to 2% in CO2 reduction
Focus Area: Efficiency Mod Solution

A customer in Malaysia was exploring ways to reduce the carbon footprint of their SGT-A35 units and help meet their decarbonization goals. Siemens Energy (SE) worked closely with the customer to evaluate the site-specific benefits and options quickly, and the resulting solution will achieve up to 2% in CO2 reduction (the equivalent of running at 6% H2 blend), 8% power increase and 2% fuel savings.
Power Generation Customer Modernizes Steam Turbines for Operational Flexibility and Emission Reduction
Focus Area: Operational Flexibility

A power generation customer was exploring ways to modernize their old fleet of 3 GE frame DRV-631 BFP turbines with very limited changes to site assets and configuration. They also wanted to achieve more power and gain more operational flexibility in terms of quicker starts and reduction in operating cost. The resulting custom-designed modification solution resulted in a 10% power increase, up to 30% CO2 reduction, faster turbine starts and extended lifecycle.
Oil & Gas Customer in Serbia Achieves up to 100% less CO2 from Compressor Drive Electrification
Focus Area: Electrification & Heat/Steam to Power
bold: Focus Area: Electrification & Heat/Steam to Power

body.text: An oil and gas customer in Serbia was exploring compressor train options to: significantly improve operational flexibility, availability and reliability; e operating costs; increase steam savings; and prepare the asset for improved remote operation capability. The solution included driver electrification, controls upgrade and changes to process and electrical connections, resulting in up to a 100% reduction in CO2, low maintenance costs and higher efficiency at part load.
Combined Heat & Power (CHP) Customer in Italy Improves Sustainability through Remote Field Service & Support
Focus Area: Digital Services

An Italian customer operating an SGT-300 in a CHP application at a military airport in Italy was unable to restart a gas turbine following maintenance. Siemens Energy was able to diagnose that the hydraulic start system (Hydrostart) had failed and would need replacing. The parts were shipped and Remote Support technology was used to assist the local team in changing out and recommissioning the Hydrostart system, resulting in improved sustainability by reducing CO2 footprint and equipment downtime.

items.title: Cybersecurity for Energy
items.h1: Perpetual vigilance for what’s mission critical
items.description: Siemens solutions for protection, detection, and monitoring to help our customers confront the growing cyber threat in the energy sector. Our offerings are part of Siemens Omnivise Digital Services.

faqs.q: Do you fear that connectivity makes you more not less vulnerable to cyber attacks?
faqs.a: Many energy companies keep their networks unconnected because they believe this makes them cyber secure. This misguided strategy will fall victim to more successful attacks, from inside and outside. Connectivity gives you visibility which provides insight.

faqs.q: Do you lack understanding of what assets to protect?
faqs.a: Many companies do not know what assets and devices exist on their OT networks. This limits their understanding of where their infrastructure is most vulnerable.

faqs.q: Do you have a shortage of in-house OT cyber expertise?
faqs.a: Most energy companies have focused on building up their IT cyber capabilities. But these cannot be simply deployed into the OT environment because of differences in the systems, data, devices, and critical dependencies. Because of this inattention to OT, cybersecurity experts who can secure complex, aging, and interdependent infra-structure are hard to find.

faqs.q: Do you have older legacy systems with exposures and vulnerabilities that are difficult to protect?
faqs.a: OT systems are older than IT systems. OT equipment, which can last decades, is often developed with proprietary systems that have exposures and vulnerabilities difficult to protect.

faqs.q: Are your security monitoring and response capabilities adequate?
faqs.a: Even if a company detects a potential intrusion into its OT cybersecurity environment, it may lack the plans or capabilities to respond effectively.

faqs.q: Do you need a multi-vendor cyber solution?
faqs.a: Cyber solutions must apply across multiple vendors to provide a single, seamless cyber program.

body.text: Siemens Energy, in partnership with Tenable, discusses current trends and challenges in industrial cybersecurity.

A conversation with Jonathan Tubb from Siemens Energy and Marty Edwards from Tenable on breaking down current trends in industrial cybersecurity and how to overcome them. We discussed the topics of; 2023 cybersecurity in review, insurance policies and trends, movement to proactive security vs. reactive security, the importance of cybersecurity for power generation, and roles and responsibilities.

Siemens Energy and Tenable are expanding our cooperation to secure critical energy infrastructure. Among other things, this means our proven Omnivise T3000 control system security protection will be enhanced with Tenable OT Security at the core.
The state of OT cybersecurity for energy and related industries

Rapid digital innovation is transforming industries worldwide. Advances in artificial intelligence are driving unprecedented electricity demand in new data centers, while cyber attackers exploit digital vulnerabilities. Energy companies are digitizing their operational technologies (OT) across both new and legacy infrastructures to optimize emissions, efficiency, and automation. The future prosperity of these industries hinges on leaders' ability to adapt. In collaboration with the Ponemon Institute, Siemens Energy surveyed critical sectors reliant on digitized OT to assess cyber threats and resilience strategies.

Our findings show that manufacturing, oil and gas, electricity, utilities, and petrochemicals face frequent and sophisticated cyberattacks on their OT systems. By raising awareness and sharing best practices, we can enhance resilience and leverage innovation while mitigating cyber risks.

Do you have older legacy systems with exposures and vulnerabilities that are difficult to protect?
OT systems are older than IT systems. OT equipment, which can last decades, is often developed with proprietary systems that have exposures and vulnerabilities difficult to protect.
Are your security monitoring and response capabilities adequate?
Even if a company detects a potential intrusion into its OT cybersecurity environment, it may lack the plans or capabilities to respond effectively.
Do you need a multi-vendor cyber solution?
Cyber solutions must apply across multiple vendors to provide a single, seamless cyber program.
If you say “yes” to one or more of the questions above, you are not alone. For energy companies, the probability of a cyber attack is nearly 100%.

Overcoming the fear of connectivity is essential because the benefits of digitalization are too great. Organizations must focus on agility and resiliency so they can respond when – not if – they are attacked.

Get answers: FAQs on power plant services
What are Siemens Energy's power plant services?

Siemens Energy's power plant services help operators improve the reliability, performance, flexibility, and long-term value of generation assets. These include maintenance and repair, remote operations, asset management, control system services, digital services and cybersecurity.
What does power plant maintenance include?

Power plant maintenance covers the scheduled, predictive and condition-based work needed to keep generating equipment reliable and efficient: inspections and planned outages, overhauls of gas turbines, steam turbines and generators, component repairs and refurbishment, control system upkeep, and the monitoring that decides when each of these is due. Siemens Energy provides these as individual services or under long-term service agreements.
How to improve power plant reliability?

Power plant reliability improves when operators identify and address potential issues before they cause equipment failures, reducing the frequency and impact of unplanned power plant outages. Remote Operations Centers, Digital Services, and Control System Services support this by providing continuous monitoring, diagnostics, predictive insights, and lifecycle support that strengthen power plant reliability, asset availability, and operational stability.
How do power plant services support energy transition goals?

Power plant services help to adapt evolving energy systems by improving operational flexibility, supporting renewable energy integration, and identifying opportunities to reduce emissions. These capabilities enable power plants to remain competitive while responding to changing market and grid requirements.
What is power plant operation and maintenance (O&M)?

Operation and maintenance, or O&M, is the combined discipline of running a plant day to day — dispatch, control room operation, performance monitoring — and keeping its equipment in serviceable condition through planned and predictive maintenance. Siemens Energy supports O&M with remote operations, asset care programs and field service, either alongside the owner's own team or as a managed service.
What is power plant asset management?

Power plant asset management is the practice of planning and prioritizing maintenance, upgrades and operating strategy around the condition, remaining life and commercial value of each asset. It combines condition data, risk assessment and lifecycle cost modelling so that spending goes where it protects revenue and availability most. Siemens Energy delivers this through Asset Care Services and the Omnivise digital portfolio.
What role does digitalization play in power plant services?

Digitalization turns operational data into actionable insights. Through remote monitoring, predictive diagnostics, and advanced analytics, power plant operators can identify performance losses, anticipate equipment issues, reduce downtime, and optimize maintenance activities.
Why are control systems important in power plants?

Power plant control systems manage and monitor the critical processes required for power generation, and they age faster than the turbines they control. Regular maintenance, software updates, lifecycle support, and cybersecurity measures help maintain system reliability, plant safety, and operational continuity.
Why is cybersecurity important for power plants?

Modern power plants rely on connected control and monitoring systems to operate safely and efficiently. Power plant cybersecurity services help protect these systems from threats, support regulatory requirements, and reduce the risk of operational disruptions caused by cyber incidents.
How can Siemens Energy's power plant services support long-term asset performance?

Siemens Energy's power plant services combine technical expertise, operational insight, and data-driven analysis to help operators improve reliability, performance, and flexibility. Through assessing plant conditions and ongoing support, these services help maximize value across the power plant lifecycle.
How do Siemens Energy's Asset Care Services support plant performance?

Asset Care Services combines operational expertise, predictive diagnostics, and performance-based service models to support asset readiness and commercial performance. The service helps operators reduce performance-related risks, improve operational flexibility, and better meet market commitments.

Digitalization turns operational data into actionable insights. Through remote monitoring, predictive diagnostics, and advanced analytics, power plant operators can identify performance losses, anticipate equipment issues, reduce downtime, and optimize maintenance activities.
Why are control systems important in power plants?

Power plant control systems manage and monitor the critical processes required for power generation, and they age faster than the turbines they control. Regular maintenance, software updates, lifecycle support, and cybersecurity measures help maintain system reliability, plant safety, and operational continuity.
Why is cybersecurity important for power plants?

Modern power plants rely on connected control and monitoring systems to operate safely and efficiently. Power plant cybersecurity services help protect these systems from threats, support regulatory requirements, and reduce the risk of operational disruptions caused by cyber incidents.
How can Siemens Energy's power plant services support long-term asset performance?

Siemens Energy's power plant services combine technical expertise, operational insight, and data-driven analysis to help operators improve reliability, performance, and flexibility. Through assessing plant conditions and ongoing support, these services help maximize value across the power plant lifecycle.
How do Siemens Energy's Asset Care Services support plant performance?

Asset Care Services combines operational expertise, predictive diagnostics, and performance-based service models to support asset readiness and commercial performance. The service helps operators reduce performance-related risks, improve operational flexibility, and better meet market commitments.

items.title: CertaLink energy certification
items.description: Certify your green products with CertaLink Energy Certificates from Siemens Energy. Benefit from our expertise & support in green certification.

faqs.q: What is the purpose of a sustainable energy certificate?
faqs.a: Sustainability certificates such as CertaLink Energy Certificates enable "Sustainability Claims" in an automated, tamper-proof, and government-approved manner. Sustainably certified products have a higher market value and offer benefits like customs and tax relief for imports and exports These green energy certifications are required by all companies that wish to market their products as sustainable. With a CertaLink certificate, you can trace the zero or low carbon origin of your products throughout the entire value chain.

faqs.q: How can I connect to the CertaLink Energy Certification Manager?
faqs.a: Whether you are planning your facility, or you have already established a production facility, you can connect to the CertaLink Energy Certification Manager. We will connect the certification manager with your Instrumentation and Control system or smart meters to access your measurement data and generate green energy certificates for your products. Plant shutdowns are usually not necessary.

faqs.q: What does CertaLink certification look like?
faqs.a: The CertaLink certification process is comparable to classic ISO certifications, but the products are continuously certified per production unit. To receive the corresponding automated issued certificate, companies must adhere to a conventional certification approach.

faqs.q: What do I need to do to prepare for CertaLink certification process?
faqs.a: We will advise you to choose the optimal certification scheme for your business purposes and prepare the certification together with you. There are document checklists depending on the selected certification scheme. A detailed list of required documents will be provided to you so that you can prepare your sustainability certification in a structured manner.

faqs.q: How do you ensure that CertaLink certificates are accepted by the government?
faqs.a: In order to apply an internationally accepted renewable energy certification standard, we are partnering with independent certification bodies, e.g. TÜV SÜD and dena, the German Energy Agency.

faqs.q: Is there a fee associated with the CertaLink Energy Certification Manager?
faqs.a: It is important to distinguish between three types of fees. An onboarding fee is charged during the connection and commissioning of the CertaLink Energy Certification Manager. A yearly membership fee is charged after completed onboarding. Later on, each certificate creation will incur a fee.

faqs.q: How do you ensure that I have control over my data and that the data is not misused?
faqs.a: The CertaLink Energy Certification Manager is based on Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT). Unlike public chains, where transactions are publicly available to everyone, in CertaLink the data is processed on a private permissioned blockchain. It means that only independent trusted and explicitly contracted node operators are participating in the network with limited access to structured data. All site data is transferred in encoded format and converted into declarations by DLT smart contracts. These declarations can be shared based on commercial operator settings.

body.text: How CertaLink certification can help you

As energy transition progresses step-by-step, the global demand for sustainable industrial manufacturing has never been higher. Companies need to demonstrate reductions in greenhouse gas emissions or verify the volume of CO2 emissions in their products. In addition, there is a growing demand to prove the sustainability of green products like sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), synthetic fuels, green steel, and other commodities.
With CertaLink Energy Certification, we can track the environmental impact of sustainable production processes along the entire product cycle.
How does CertaLink Energy Certification work?

Developed with innovation partners TÜV SÜD and the German Energy Agency (dena), CertaLink Energy Certification uses blockchain technology to connect physical assets to digital decentralized infrastructure. It tracks the low and zero carbon energy from source to consumption along the value chain, validating the energy's origin plus providing detailed insights and attributes. As a result of automated and tamper-proof recording and tracking of energy-specific data, a CertaLink certificate is valid around the world through the entire low or zero carbon value chain.

faqs.q: How much power do data centers use?
faqs.a: Data centers consume a significant amount of power, and their energy usage can vary widely based on several factors, including size, design, efficiency, and the type of equipment used. Small data centers may use 1-5 MW, while larger ones can consume 20MW to over 100MW-2000MW.

faqs.q: What is the rated power in a data center?
faqs.a: A data center's rated power, usually measured in megawatts (MW), refers to the maximum amount of electrical power that the facility can deliver to its IT equipment, cooling systems, and other infrastructure at any given time.

faqs.q: What is the power supply of a data center?
faqs.a: Data center power supplies typically come from the local electrical grid which provides the primary source of power. To ensure continuous operation during power outages, data centers often have backup generators (usually diesel or natural gas) that can provide power until utility service is restored. In locations where the grid is unavailable or unable to supply sufficient power, data center also have onsite power generation to deliver continuous power to the data center.

faqs.q: Can data center use renewable energy?
faqs.a: Yes, some data centers are incorporating renewable energy sources, such as solar, wind and hydro power, to power their operations and reduce their carbon footprint.

faqs.q: What is the primary function of a power distribution (PDU) in a data center
faqs.a: The primary function of a PDU in a data center is to distribute electrical power efficiently to multiple IT devices like servers, routers, and switches, ensuring a consistent and reliable power supply to all equipment within the data center.

To keep pace, while other industries are also drawing from limited global capacity, data center operators and developers are turning to Siemens Energy to step up to the challenges and provide solutions. Siemens Energy understands the specific requirements of data centers and has developed an extensive portfolio of technologies to address these needs. By leveraging these strengths, Siemens Energy supports the development of data centers that meet current operational requirements while advancing toward greater sustainability and connectivity for the future.

body.text: Metals and mining industry solutions are the cornerstone of modern engineering and construction, integral to everything from skyscrapers and automobiles to infrastructure and machinery. As global demand has surged over the past five decades, the industry faces pressing challenges. Primary metals production is a significant contributor to greenhouse gas emissions. Generating more than three times the emissions of the aviation industry, the steel industry produces an average of 1.8 tons of carbon dioxide for every ton of steel produced.
bold: 1.8 tons of carbon dioxide for every ton of steel

body.text: Embracing sustainable practices and innovative technologies is essential to meet rising demands while minimizing our environmental impact.
How will the metals and mining industry adapt to the changing world?

The industry is undergoing the current challenges of increasing demand, strong market competition, changing regulations and changing value chains. This addresses fuel, heat and power supplies and requires integrated electrical solutions to balance any type of plant. Given the nature of metal processes and the complexity and fragmentation of their value chain, there is no simple or single solution to decarbonize the industry. We understand the challenging requirements of the metal industry and our diverse portfolio of technologies supports the further growth of this heads-on.

Together, let's shape a decarbonized future, where we not only meet today's production demands but also significantly reduce our carbon footprint. By leveraging innovative technologies, we can pave the way for a more sustainable and interconnected metal industry.
Discover decarbonization offerings to support your journey to net-zero and reduce emissions via a stepwise approach for mining and metal industry solutions.

body.text: Powering the mining and metal industry on both routes

The Blast Furnace-Basic Oxygen Furnace (BF-BOF) processes, known as the primary route, accounts for 70% of global steel production. The steel production in blast furnaces requires industrial electrification and energy efficiency combined with waste heat recovery.

Utilizing iron sponge and steel scrap as main feedstock, the Direct Reduced Iron - Electric Arc Furnace route (DRI-EAF) which uses natural gas or hydrogen, eliminating up to 80% of CO2 in steel production. Fuel shifts within the steel industry are relevant to transform brownfield steel plants to address future needs on this secondary route.

body.text: Electric arc furnaces (EAF) power compensation
ActiFeed PLUS
Given the dynamic load behaviors of EAFs, which can consume up to 300 MVA, Siemens Energy's SVC PLUS® STATCOM technology offers different solutions to perfectly fit your needs.

Discover the future of energy supply with ActiFeed PLUS, our innovative solution to feed three-phase electric arc furnaces maximizing energy efficiency while minimizing operating costs and environmental impact. Utilizing PLUS® technology in an advanced Modular Multilevel Matrix Converter (M3C), ActiFeed PLUS ensures precise power control for stable arcs and optimal energy utilization, resulting in reduced power-on times and unprecedented grid stability. SVC PLUS® complements this by providing a cutting-edge STATCOM solution that enhances power quality. Each of these technologies enables modern steel plants to boost productivity, lower costs, and seamlessly meet stringent grid requirements while ensuring stability and reliability in power systems.
ActiFeed PLUS Fly Over
SVC PLUS® (STATCOM) for better industrial load compensation
bold: SVC PLUS® (STATCOM) for better industrial load compensation

body.text: Large electrical consumers in industrial processes often show a very dynamic behavior. Looking at the most extreme case of electrical loads worldwide, Electrical Arc Furnaces (EAFs) – where a single unit can have a consumption of up to around 300 MVA (the consumption of a city of 300.000 inhabitants) – their load characteristic is extremely dynamic and stochastic, creating a number of disturbances to the feeding grid, such as fast voltage fluctuations causing the phenomenon of flickering of light, bad power factor and asymmetric loading of the 3 phases of the supply system, as well generation of harmonics due to the non linear current of the electric arc. To counteract the disturbances of such industrial loads, an innovative and versatile compensation solution for enhancing power quality is required - SVC PLUS® provides the ideal solution. Our advanced STATCOM (static synchronous compensator) with modular multilevel converter (MMC) technology provides additional benefits compared to conventional solutions for load compensation.
SVC PLUS® for industrial applications - introduction:
bold: SVC PLUS® for industrial applications - introduction:

body.text: While conventional SVC installations already provide a highly dynamic solution for power quality improvement at the the grid connection point of an industrial power distribution system, the modular multilevel system SVC PLUS® is even faster and offers multiple additional benefits. Depending on the size and characteristics of the load and the utility regulations, we offer different SVC PLUS® concepts to mitigate the unwanted impact of the load to the grid.
Have a closer look at our iSVC PLUS® layouts and 3D experiences:

Compression

Integrally geared compressors and single-stage radial compressors are essential in the steel industry, particularly in blast furnace (BF) processes. These compressors supply fresh air and facilitate oxygen delivery from air separation units (ASUs) to the basic oxygen furnace (BOF), helping to reduce carbon content in pig iron. In the direct reduced iron (DRI) production, compressors manage critical gas streams, including hydrogen and carbon monoxide, under challenging conditions. Our offerings support carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) by compressing captured CO₂ for storage or utilization, ensuring efficient and sustainable operations in steel manufacturing. We provide advanced hydrogen or CO₂ compressor solutions tailored to these specific needs, ensuring efficient and reliable operation in DRI plants.
Waste heat recovery system (WHRS)

A considerable portion of the energy consumed in the steel industry is rejected as waste heat from the electric arc furnace (EAF). Utilizing this heat impacts the efficiency of production significantly by reducing operating costs, feeding extra electricity to the grid or increasing the plant's productivity. It also presents great opportunities to increase the industry's competitiveness and sustainable operation through a reduction in emissions.

WHRS includes a reduction in the carbon footprint of steel plant operations, lower production and operating costs, and supports organizations ESG goals to support Scope 2. Our technology uses residual heat from the exhaust gases generated in steel manufacturing process and has potential to generate electricity. Electric power expenses can account for up to 40% of total operating cost of EAF plant.

WHRS can reduce the electrical energy consumtion, variable costs and improve margins. It can also save up to 60 m3/ hr of water currently used in cooling down the electric arc furnace off-gas in water jacketed ducts and corresponds to evaporation losses in cooling towers, thus contributing to sustainable development and improve your plant efficiency.
bold: save up to 60 m3/ hr of water
contributing to sustainable development and improve your plant efficiency.

body.text: Waste heat integration in carbon capture

CO2 capturing today is often done by a post-combustion amine-based carbon capture system. A typical challenge is that compressors are required for achieving maximum efficiency, which means the temperature level and the heat generation are intended to be kept as low as possible. On the other hand, an amine process requires high amounts of LP steam.
Benefits of heat integration for high process steam recovery:

items: With the compressor operated at a higher temperature level, significant amounts of LP steam can be produced by recovery of compression heat, only requiring slightly more compressor driver power (Coefficient of Performance of up to 6.0)
Electric motor driven compressor with heat recovery
Heat recovered is redirected back to CO2 capture (CC) system

body.text: It is often overlooked that the carbon capture units require a considerable amount of extra heat and steam to be operated effectively. To address the increased steam demand, Siemens Energy service experts evaluate two potential solutions:

items: Installation of an additional steam turbine to cover the extra heat
Demand or modification of the existing steam turbine

body.text: Green hydrogen production

Hydrogen production is crucial for turning traditional steelmaking processes to sustainable green steelmaking. Electrolyzers play a key role by providing green hydrogen using green electricity from renewable sources. This hydrogen is then compressed using compressors to increase its energy density, making it suitable for storage and transportation. The compressed hydrogen can be used in direct reduction processes to convert iron ore into steel, significantly reducing carbon emissions compared to traditional methods. This integration of electrolyzers and compressors in hydrogen production supports the metal industry's shift towards more sustainable practices.

Green steel is produced using innovative technologies to drastically reduce the carbon footprint of steel manufacturing. The innovative approach replaces fossil fuels with renewable energy sources and green hydrogen, significantly lowering CO2 emissions.

In parallel, gas turbines for industrial power generation for primary metal production facilities support future energy systems by providing flexible power to compensate for solar and wind intermittency. Cutting-edge hydrogen mixing technologies enable gas turbines to operate on hydrogen blends, reducing carbon emissions and future-proofing infrastructure.
