faqs.q: What solutions does Siemens Energy offer for the oil and gas industry?
faqs.a: Siemens Energy delivers integrated solutions across upstream, midstream, and downstream operations, including industrial and aeroderivative gas turbines, advanced compressors, electrification systems, automation and digitalization platforms, and comprehensive lifecycle services.

faqs.q: How do Siemens Energy gas turbines support oil and gas operations?
faqs.a: Siemens Energy gas turbines provide reliable power generation for onshore and offshore applications, including gas processing plants, refineries, and FPSOs. They also serve as mechanical drives for compressors and pumps, offering low NOx emissions, broad fuel flexibility, and exceptional reliability.

faqs.q: What types of compressors does Siemens Energy provide?
faqs.a: The portfolio includes reciprocating, single-shaft, and integrally geared compressors engineered for upstream gas gathering, midstream pipeline transport, and downstream refining. These systems are certified to API 618, API 617, and ISO 13631 standards, ensuring durability, energy efficiency, and reduced emissions.

faqs.q: How does Siemens Energy support decarbonization in oil and gas?
faqs.a: Siemens Energy offers electrification solutions, low-emission technologies, power-from-shore systems for offshore platforms, and integration-ready infrastructure for carbon capture—helping operators reduce emissions, lower costs, and meet sustainability goals.

faqs.q: What digital and automation solutions for oil and gas industry are available?
faqs.a: Siemens Energy provides AI-enhanced asset management, predictive maintenance, remote diagnostics (RDS), terminal management systems, process control and SCADA systems, and intelligent automation for unmanned operations—enabling real-time monitoring, data-driven decisions, and optimized performance.

faqs.q: Can Siemens Energy support offshore oil and gas operations?
faqs.a: Yes, Siemens Energy offers gas turbine packages designed for offshore power generation and mechanical drive applications, compression systems and offshore electrification via HVDC and HVAC,all engineered for harsh environments, compact spaces, and high reliability.

faqs.q: What oil and gas services does Siemens Energy provide throughout the asset lifecycle?
faqs.a: Services include installation and commissioning, comprehensive maintenance programs, upgrades and modernization, emergency response, remote diagnostics, and 24/7 expert support in multiple languages—ensuring maximum uptime, asset reliability, and operational efficiency.

faqs.q: How does Siemens Energy enhance safety and reliability in oil and gas?
faqs.a: Through advanced control systems, condition monitoring, safety-integrated designs, zero harm policies with a right-to-stop-work culture, and digital tools that enable predictive analytics and real-time visibility—minimizing risk, downtime, and operational disruptions.

faqs.a: Offshore electrification replaces traditional gas turbine generation with cleaner power-from-shore solutions, significantly reducing emissions and fuel costs, lowering noise levels, and improving operational efficiency while supporting decarbonization and regulatory compliance.

faqs.a: Digital twins and predictive analytics provide real-time performance insights, optimize asset management, enable proactive maintenance strategies, reduce unplanned downtime, and enhance visibility across the entire energy value chain—driving productivity, sustainability, and cost savings.

items.description: Integrated FPSO solutions for safe, efficient floating production with advanced power, compression, and digital systems.

body.text: Floating Production, Storage and Offloading (FPSOs) offshore production vessels are a key solution for developing offshore oil and gas fields, particularly in deep water and extended distance from shore. As self‑contained production facilities at sea, FPSOs enable the efficient processing of hydrocarbons whilst being entirely self sufficient for power generation and commercial operations meaning that safety and reliability are key.

For Floating production, storage and offloading (FPSO) projects, Siemens Energy brings together the technologies, expertise and integration capabilities needed to shape high-performing offshore assets. With a fully integrated portfolio spanning power generation, compression, electrification, automation and digital solutions, Siemens Energy help customers move from complexity to clarity, reducing risk, optimizing performance and creating long-term value across the asset lifecycle. As a systems integrator, Siemens Energy can offer the complete package – gas turbines, compressors and system integration.
Customer challenges

FPSO operators face complex technical and operational challenges throughout the asset lifecycle whilst ensuring performance demands and managing strict space and weight limitations on the topside. These include achieving high reliability and availability in isolated locations, ensuring safe operation under harsh conditions. At the same time seeking to improve reduce emissions and comply with increasingly stringent regulatory and sustainability requirements. Addressing these challenges requires robust, highly integrated solutions designed for long‑term performance, reliability and environmental responsibility.

Siemens Energy offers a comprehensive portfolio of integrated solutions for FPSOs, designed to support safe, efficient and reliable offshore operations across the full lifecycle of the asset. The portfolio combines power generation, compression, electrification, automation and digital technologies, engineered to meet the specific requirements of offshore production environments. With a focus on high availability, compact design and long‑term performance, Siemens Energy solutions help FPSO operators optimise operations, reduce emissions and ensure dependable energy supply under the most demanding conditions.
Solutions Portfolio

items: Compressors
Gas turbines for power generation

body.text: Compression is a critical element of FPSO operations, supporting key processes such as gas lift, gas injection, fuel gas supply, export gas handling and CO₂ reinjection. Siemens Energy provides a broad portfolio of centrifugal and reciprocating compressor solutions specifically engineered to meet the demanding requirements of offshore production environments, including high availability, compact design and long term operational reliability.
Centrifugal compressor solutions

Siemens Energy centrifugal compressors are widely deployed on FPSOs for high flow, continuous duty applications. Based on proven technologies, these compressors are optimised for applications including gas injection, export compression and CO₂ reinjection. Compact, high pressure centrifugal compressor solutions enable challenging production to high reservoir pressures while reducing overall footprint and weight, a key advantage for topside integration. Our DATUM compressor has been successfully applied on FPSOs operating in high pressure, corrosive conditions, deep water and pre salt fields, delivering reliable performance under high pressures and demanding process conditions.
Motor driven and all electric compression trains
bold: Motor driven and all electric compression trains

body.text: To support electrification strategies and emissions reduction goals, Siemens Energy offers motor driven compressor trains for FPSO applications. These solutions are a core element of all electric FPSO concepts and are used across main gas compression, gas lift, booster sales, gas re-injection and CO₂ compression and sequestration services. Electric motor driven compressors enable high efficiency, reduced maintenance requirements and seamless integration with advanced power management and automation systems. The changing market landscape underscores the importance of electric compression for improved operational costs and reduced greenhouse gas emissions over the lifecycle of the asset.
Reciprocating compressor solutions

For applications requiring high pressure at lower flow rates or wide operational flexibility, Siemens Energy typically supplies High speed reciprocating compressors for FPSO use. These compressors are well suited for fuel gas, flash gas and gas lift services where variable flow conditions and high pressure ratios are required. The portfolio includes electrically driven and engine driven configurations, designed in accordance with international offshore standards and classification requirements.
Integrated compressor packages and lifecycle support
bold: Integrated compressor packages and lifecycle support

body.text: All compressor solutions for FPSOs are delivered as fully integrated packages, including drivers, controls, auxiliaries and safety systems. Siemens Energy applies a holistic engineering approach to optimize footprint and performance, simplify installation and reduce commissioning time. Advanced turbomachinery control systems ensure safe and reliable operation, including anti surge protection, performance monitoring and seamless integration with the FPSO control architecture. Comprehensive lifecycle services support long term availability and operational excellence throughout the lifetime of the FPSO.

Offshore oil and gas facilities, including FPSO units, demand power generation systems that balance high availability, compact footprint, power density and cost efficiency while maintaining flexibility to accommodate future technologies. Siemens Energy evaluates distributed offshore power generation and compression drive architectures based on modular industrial and aeroderivative gas turbines for use in harsh conditions, where these attributes are paramount, whilst ensuring that technology integration potential with future technologies such as combined cycle, carbon capture, and exhaust gas recirculation is in mind.

Siemens Energy analyses consider various operating profiles, emission levels, start capabilities, and overall footprint demanded for each application, as well as considering customer experience and specifications.

Using representative offshore load profiles and redundancy philosophies, Siemens Energy can combine these turbine classes in a distributed configuration enabling optimized sizing, improved operational flexibility, and reduced installed power margins. Capital expenditure impacts are evaluated by comparing equipment cost, topside weight, footprint, and balance-of-plant requirements against conventional centralized generation concepts.

The inherent modularity of the gas turbines enables phased installation, simplified maintenance strategies, and improved availability through redundancy without oversizing individual units. Furthermore, the selected turbine characteristics support integration with emerging technologies and low-carbon fuel blends.
Services for FPSO applications

Siemens Energy provides a comprehensive service portfolio to support the safe, reliable and efficient operation of FPSOs throughout their entire lifecycle. From commissioning and maintenance to upgrades, modernisation and long‑term service programmes, Siemens Energy services are designed to maximise availability, optimise performance and extend asset life in demanding offshore environments. Backed by global service expertise and deep domain knowledge, these services help FPSO operators reduce downtime, manage operational risk and adapt their assets to evolving performance and sustainability requirements.

faqs.q: What is a thermal power plant?
faqs.a: A thermal power plant generates electricity by converting heat energy – typically from the combustion of fuels such as natural gas, oil, biomass, waste or coal, or from nuclear reactions – into mechanical energy using gas turbines, steam turbines or reciprocating engines. This mechanical energy is then transformed into electrical energy by a generator.

faqs.q: Is thermal power eco-friendly?
faqs.a: The environmental impact of thermal power plants varies depending on plant type, age, fuel source, and operating conditions. Modern gas fired, biomass, and waste to energy plants achieve low greenhouse gas emissions and minimal harmful pollutants due to advanced combustion and emissions control technologies. Nuclear plants emit no greenhouse gases or combustion related air pollutants.

faqs.q: What are the advantages of thermal power plants?
faqs.a: Key advantages include high reliability, the ability to supply stable baseload or fast‑responding peak power on demand, strong grid‑stabilizing capabilities, proven and mature technology, operational flexibility, and compatibility with a wide range of fuels and combined heat‑and‑power configurations for higher overall efficiency.

faqs.q: Which fuel is used in thermal power plants?
faqs.a: Thermal power plants can use natural gas, oil, biomass, coal, waste or waste-derived fuels, or nuclear fuel, depending on plant type.

faqs.q: How do gas-fired power plants support the energy transition?
faqs.a: Gas-fired power plants offer lower CO₂ emissions compared to coal-based plants, provide flexible operation to balance variable wind and solar generation, and can be adapted for hydrogen co-firing to further decarbonize power generation.

faqs.q: Can thermal power plants work with renewable energy?
faqs.a: Yes, thermal power plants can operate on renewable fuels such as biomass. They also complement variable renewable energy sources by providing flexible backup capacity and essential grid stabilizing services, such as inertia and frequency support, to maintain stability and reliability when wind or solar output fluctuate.

faqs.q: What services does Siemens Energy provide for thermal power plants?
faqs.a: Siemens Energy delivers the full scope from equipment supply like gas and steam turbines to complete power plants, including I&C, modernization, lifecycle service, maintenance, and remote operational support to enhance reliability and reduce downtime.

body.text: Thermal power plants remain essential components of modern energy systems, even as the share of renewable generation increases. Due to the inherent variability of solar and wind output, thermal plants provide the reliable, dispatchable capacity required to maintain grid stability and secure power supply. Siemens Energy offers a wide range of solutions, products, and services for thermal power generation.
Types of thermal power plants
Thermal power plants generate electricity by converting heat from burning fuels such as natural gas, oil, biomass, waste, or coal, or from nuclear reactions.

The portfolio includes gas‑fired power plant solutions for simple‑cycle, combined‑cycle, cogeneration, and district‑heating applications, along with steam turbines for nuclear and biomass facilities. They are deployed in both industrial and utility‑scale installations and operate across base‑load, load‑following, and peaking modes.
Gas-fired power generation

Gas fired power plants can be either simple or open cycle plants, or combined cycle power plants (CCPP) which integrate both gas and steam turbines, for high efficiency. Combined heat and power plants (CHP) efficiently produce both electricity and thermal energy.

Gas-fired power plants help to reduce CO2 emissions and support renewable energy integration. Siemens Energy offers the full scope of supply from different gas turbine and steam turbine types to full power plants like open cycle for peak power or combined cycle for base load as well as I&C and service and maintenance offerings.

body.text: Combined cycle power plants (CCPP)

Combined Cycle Power Plants (CCPP) integrate advanced gas and steam turbines to achieve efficiencies in excess of 64%, significantly lower emissions and the flexibility to match output to demand. Visit website
Open cycle peaker plants

Peaker plants address the need for dispatchable, flexible and responsive power generation. They are designed to come online when power is needed most, with fast start-up capabilities and high ramp rates. Visit website
Combined heat and power plants (CHP plants)
Combined heat and power (CHP) plants generate electricity and heat from a single fuel source, utilizing the waste heat produced during electricity generation. Visit website
Hydrogen-fired & H2 co-fired planst

Siemens Energy provides hydrogen‑ready power plants equipped with advanced gas turbines capable of operating on fuel mixes up to 100% hydrogen. The plants support low‑carbon power generation, enhancing decarbonization potential and future‑proofing thermal power assets. Visit website
Floating power plants

Mobile floating power plants provide fast, efficient power with reduced pollution and noise disturbance, making optimal use of scarce resources. The evolution of open and combined cycle power plants from land to sea is based on Siemens Energy's proven gas and steam turbine portfolio. Visit website
Nuclear power plant solutions

Nuclear power plants provide a dependable source of low-carbon electricity that complements the variability of renewable energy sources like wind and solar. Siemens Energy offers steam turbine island solutions, I&C and digital solutions, service and maintenance for nuclear power plants and small modular reactors (SMR).
Biomass, waste-to-energy, concentrated solar power

Siemens Energy is at the forefront of integrating biomass and concentrated solar power (CSP) into energy generation, providing comprehensive steam cycle solutions that encompass steam turbines, instrumentation and control systems, as well as service and maintenance options.

faqs.q: Why is renewable energy essential for the energy transition?
faqs.a: Renewable sources like solar, wind, hydropower, and biofuels are vital for reducing carbon emissions and limiting global warming to 1.5°C. They enable sustainable, environmentally responsible energy systems while decreasing dependence on fossil fuels.

faqs.q: How much renewable energy capacity needs to be added by 2030?
faqs.a: According to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), the world must add approximately 1,000 GW of renewable energy capacity every year until 2030 to meet climate targets and triple global renewable capacity to at least 11 terawatts.

faqs.q: What are the main challenges facing renewable energy deployment?
faqs.a: Key challenges include intermittency (solar and wind depend on weather conditions), energy storage limitations, grid infrastructure requirements, land use, regulatory frameworks, and the need for long-distance power transmission.

faqs.q: How does Siemens Energy address the intermittency of renewable energy?
faqs.a: Siemens Energy provides energy storage solutions, advanced grid access technologies, and power transmission and distribution systems that help balance supply and demand, ensuring reliable energy delivery even when renewable generation fluctuates.

faqs.q: What is green hydrogen and why is it important in renewable energy?
faqs.a: Green hydrogen is produced by splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using electrolysis powered by renewable energy. It's essential for decarbonizing hard-to-electrify sectors like heavy industry, shipping, and aviation, offering a clean, sustainable fuel alternative.

faqs.q: What electrolyzer technology does Siemens Energy use for green hydrogen production?
faqs.a: Siemens Energy's Elyzer product family uses Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) electrolysis, ideal for harnessing volatile renewable energy from wind and solar. PEM electrolyzers deliver high efficiency, superior gas quality, easy operation, and low maintenance.

faqs.q: Can gas turbines support the renewable energy transition?
faqs.a: Yes. Siemens Energy's gas turbines are designed to be future-proof and can run on hydrogen. By 2030, the company aims to increase the hydrogen fuel-mix percentage to 100%, making gas turbines a sustainable bridge technology during the energy transition.

faqs.q: How does Siemens Energy support large-scale hydrogen production?
faqs.a: Siemens Energy offers modular electrolyzer systems that scale up to gigawatt capacity, supporting massive green hydrogen production for industrial applications. Their automated plants use robotics and digitalization for efficiency and cost optimization.

faqs.q: What role does energy storage play in renewable energy systems?
faqs.a: Energy storage is critical for managing intermittency by capturing excess renewable energy when production exceeds demand and releasing it when needed. Technologies like batteries and pumped hydro storage help stabilize grids and ensure continuous power supply.

faqs.q: How is Siemens Energy contributing to building a sustainable hydrogen economy?
faqs.a: Siemens Energy collaborates with government, academia, and industry partners to create scalable, profitable hydrogen solutions. With expertise across industrial, mobility, and energy sectors, they provide dependable end-to-end solutions for green hydrogen production, transportation, and utilization.

faqs.q: What renewable energy solutions does Siemens Energy offer?
faqs.a: Siemens Energy provides end-to-end renewable energy solutions spanning power generation, grid access, storage, and green hydrogen, enabling customers to integrate solar, wind, hydropower, and biomass into robust, low-carbon energy systems.

faqs.q: Which renewable energy products are part of Siemens Energy’s portfolio?
faqs.a: The portfolio includes components and systems such as renewable-ready gas turbines, grid connection equipment, storage technologies, and electrolyzers for green hydrogen, all designed to support large-scale deployment of renewable energy products worldwide.

faqs.q: What is air separation?
faqs.a: Air separation is a process used to separate atmospheric air into its primary components, mainly nitrogen, oxygen, and argon. This is typically achieved through methods such as cryogenic distillation, pressure swing adsorption (PSA), or membrane separation.

faqs.q: What is the role of compression in air separation?
faqs.a: Compression in air separation increases the air pressure, facilitating efficient cooling and liquefaction, which enhances the separation of gases like nitrogen, oxygen, and argon.

faqs.q: What are air separation plants?
faqs.a: Air separation plants are industrial facilities designed to separate atmospheric air into its primary components, mainly nitrogen, oxygen, and argon, using processes like cryogenic distillation, pressure swing adsorption (PSA), or membrane separation. These plants produce high-purity gases for various applications in industries such as healthcare, manufacturing, and electronics.

faqs.q: How do compressors work in air separation plants?
faqs.a: In air separation plants, compressors work by increasing the pressure of the incoming air. Best efficiency is reached by using integrally geared compressors, this technology enables intercooling after each impeller and can be applied over a wide range of flows, from 1000m³/h up to 1,500,000m³/h. This high-pressure air is then cooled to very low temperatures, causing it to liquefy. The liquefied air is subsequently separated into its components, nitrogen, oxygen, and argon, based on their boiling points. Compressors are essential for achieving the necessary pressure and temperature conditions for efficient gas separation.

faqs.q: What are air separation units (ASU)?
faqs.a: Air Separation Units (ASUs) are industrial systems designed to divide atmospheric air into its main components—primarily nitrogen, oxygen, and argon. They achieve this through methods such as cryogenic distillation, pressure swing adsorption (PSA), or membrane separation. ASUs are crucial for producing high-purity gases used in various sectors, including healthcare, manufacturing, and electronics.

body.text: Providing a future-proof source of electricity and contributing to lower CO₂ emissions, power produced from biomass is increasingly economically viable. The interests of operators and investors, on the one hand, and those of utilities and grids, on the other, are becoming more closely aligned. This is because ensuring a stable power supply as well as the financial success of the power plant are common goals.
Siemens Energy to electrify first-of-its-kind biorefinery in Germany

The biorefinery will be the first industrial-scale facility of its type ever built. It will apply novel process innovations to sustainably convert 100 percent wood into bio-based mono-ethylene glycol (MEG), mono-propylene glycol (MPG) as well as renewable functional fillers (RFF).
Centered on biomass – an integral part of the industry
Biomass is green power

With more widespread environmental awareness and the resultant striving for “green” lifestyles, biomass energy for both industry and electricity providers is a reliable – and sustainable – source of baseload power.
It also helps in meeting environmental targets, absorbing more CO₂ than it emits, and efficient equipment used in power generation leads to fewer emissions at the plant site.
Biomass is a relatively cheap base load and, depending on the local regulations, surplus electricity produced from it can be fed back to the grid, making it even more economically viable.
Closed-cycle economies
Installing a biomass power plant to burn the on-site waste that occurs as a by-product of industrial processes closes the factory input cycle.
It also eliminates the need for waste disposal, lowers energy costs and maintains a high availability of the power supply.

Incinerating renewables is thus a further step toward sustainability and toward a closed-cycle economy. These by-products need no additional processing, further strengthening the financial feasibility of the biomass plant.
Favored by investors
The possibility of running a biomass plant on diverse feedstocks adds to the viability of such projects while ensuring the availability of the fuel supply.

Apart from achieving maximum output with a minimum of life-cycle costs, another decisive economic factor is the need for appropriate frameworks already in the country concerned, regulating such variables as electricity prices, the level of tipping tax, and funding.
Why Siemens Energy for biomass solutions?
Flexible, reliable operation
With their leading efficiency profile and minimal outages, our turbines maximize the amount of electricity generated while further reducing a plant's lifetime emissions footprint.
Lowest lifecycle costs, reliable equipment
All our turbines offer a long life cycle thanks to reliable equipment that is backed by our global service.
Strong reputation and references
Thanks to our long list of references we can help gain acceptance for biomass energy among the authorities and the local population.
Professional project development
We can support you from the very beginning with our technical consulting and expertise, dealing with all the parties involved and avoiding any complications.

body.text: At Siemens Energy, we believe in the potential of Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS). Advancing this technology is essential for a sustainable future. By partnering with customers, CCUS providers, and policymakers, we lead in decarbonizing the energy sector. Together, we are building a more sustainable world for future generations. Let's turn ambition into action and create a cleaner, greener planet.
The climate imperative for Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage

To effectively combat climate change and reach net-zero emissions, a multitude of technologies are essential. CCUS will play a pivotal role in reducing CO₂ emissions by leveraging existing infrastructure. The International Energy Agency (IEA) underscores the necessity of CCUS, emphasizing the need to capture approximately 1 gigatonne of CO₂ annually by 2030 to align with international climate objectives, such as those set by the Paris Agreement. Integration design studies are important in refining CO₂ capture plants in terms of size, cost, and efficiency. Our equipment, including steam and gas compressors, facilitates CCUS deployment across the entire spectrum, encompassing capture, storage, and utilization. The process of capturing CO₂ after combustion is notably energy-demanding, relying on electricity and low-pressure steam usually sourced from the power plant, which can diminish the plant's overall efficiency and power output. By optimizing steam turbine configurations and harnessing waste heat from CO₂ capture and compression, we can improve the power plant output, efficiency, and functionality of these plants.

items: Reducing emissions from power generation and industry
Enabling clean hydrogen production
Direct air capture and bioenergy with CCS (BECCS)
Solutions for transportation and storage of CO₂

body.text: CCUS can be added to new build or be retrofitted to existing fossil fuel-based power plants and industrial facilities, capturing CO₂ emissions that would otherwise be released into the atmosphere. This is particularly important for sectors where emissions are hard to abate, such as cement and steel production.

Hydrogen is a clean fuel that can be produced using fossil fuels with CCUS, known as blue hydrogen. This process captures the CO₂ produced during hydrogen production, making it a low-carbon alternative to green hydrogen produced from renewable energy sources until enough resources for green hydrogen are constructed.

CCUS technologies can also capture CO₂ directly with direct air capture (DAC) or from bioenergy processes (BECCS). These methods can remove CO₂ from the atmosphere, helping to balance emissions that are difficult to eliminate. Furthermore the synergistic approach of Direct Air Capture combined with carbon sequestration (DACCS) is acknowledged for its potential to generate negative emissions, representing a robust, enduring approach to Carbon Dioxide Removal.

In addition to our comprehensive approach to Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS), we are also focusing on the system design aspects, including liquefication and drying. These processes are crucial for the efficient handling and storage of captured CO₂. Liquefication allows for the CO₂ to be transported more easily and stored in a more compact form, while drying ensures that the CO₂ is free from moisture, which can cause corrosion and other issues in storage and transportation systems.
Partner with Siemens Energy to decarbonize the energy sector

The global energy landscape largely relies on fossil fuels, by 2035, DNV estimates ~30% of electricity will still come from fossil fuels (Energy Transition Outlook 2024). An abrupt switch to renewables is not yet feasible. CCUS-equipped gas-fired power generation complements renewable energy, ensuring availability and security when renewables are offline. We are leading in the development of CCUS technology, addressing climate change and supporting the transition to a low-carbon future.

We have explored carbon management technologies for decades and continue to find ways to support the energy sector's transition with CCUS. Our extensive knowledge of energy systems allows us to work with industry partners to integrate carbon capture technology and create comprehensive CCUS solutions.
Tailored carbon capture solutions for a sustainable future

Different technologies cater to various industries' needs, addressing their specific emission sources and regulatory environments. We collaborate with leading carbon capture providers to deliver efficient, reliable customized solutions.

Our strategic partnerships, combined with our extensive experience in energy technology, enable us to access cutting-edge technologies from leading suppliers. This allows us to concentrate on our core competency of integrating power plants with capture plants, thereby ensuring optimal efficiency and asset utilization.

What is Carbon Capture, Usage, and Storage (CCUS)?

CCUS is a key technological innovation aimed at reducing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions. By capturing CO₂ from industrial processes, air and power and heat generation, CCUS prevents this greenhouse gas from impacting climate change. The captured CO₂ is then either repurposed in various industries or safely stored underground. CCUS is essential for lowering emissions in challenging sectors like steel and cement manufacturing and is a complement of sustainable low-carbon electricity and hydrogen production. As a method for atmospheric CO₂ removal, CCUS is integral to achieving net-zero emissions and ensuring long-term energy security.
How does CCUS technology work?

Advanced capture technologies such as pre-combustion, post-combustion, DAC and oxy-fuel combustion of CO₂ from the atmosphere are employed to intercept CO₂ emissions at their source, including industrial and power generation facilities.
Once captured, CO₂ can be put to work in various sectors, being used in the chemical, and food and beverage industries, thus turning a waste product into a valuable commodity.
Transportation to secure storage locations and subsequent underground sequestration of CO₂ in geological formations ensures that it is contained and does not re-enter the atmosphere.
Transforming challenges into opportunities: The promising future of CCUS

CCUS offers significant potential for a sustainable future. Although high costs, infrastructure needs, and regulatory uncertainties pose challenges, they also drive innovation. Government support, such as tax credits and carbon pricing, can spur progress. Additionally, international collaboration and investment in R&D are essential for advancing CCUS technologies, enhancing their efficiency and cost-effectiveness.
Embracing these opportunities will promote CCUS adoption, cut carbon emissions, and support a sustainable planet.

As a trusted partner, we help our customers select the most appropriate technologies for their specific needs. By partnering with leading carbon capture providers, we combine our energy technology and infrastructure expertise with their specialized knowledge to deliver efficient and reliable customized solutions.
Sustainable alternative fuels for gas turbines

Transform your energy systems with hydrogen, methanol, ammonia, and HVO. Our gas turbines running on sustainable alternative fuels offer flexible, carbon-neutral solutions to complement intermittent renewable energy sources like wind and solar.

items.title: Coal-to-Gas Conversion for Power Plants
items.description: Convert coal plants to efficient gas to cut CO₂ emissions by up to 70%. Use existing assets now and prepare for future hydrogen adoption.

faqs.q: Step 1: Design concept
faqs.a: Understanding customer’s market environment, the regional energy system and regulatory framework in order to create a customized cost-optimized, efficient, or flexible solution, while aiming at the same time at integrating as many existing assets as possible.

faqs.q: Step 2: Geometrical fit
faqs.a: Analyzing how to integrate the new equipment – such as gas turbines or generators – fit into the existing plant layout and infrastructure. Especially for indoor solutions, it’s important to analyze how existing foundations, piping and connections can be reused, while ensuring the new setup will work smoothly and safely.

faqs.q: Step 3: Thermodynamic fit
faqs.a: Identifying the best configuration with the best thermodynamic fit in order to match the future operating regime with the intended business model. This can involve various, far-reaching measures, as, e.g., the steam cycle of a conventional steam power plant differs fundamentally from that of a CCPP.

faqs.q: Step 4: Steam turbine retrofit
faqs.a: Adapting the existing steam turbine and generator to operating parameters of a combined cycle plant. This may concern especially higher temperatures – up to 600°C and more for a steam turbine – that modern CCPPs use today.

body.text: 75% of global CO₂ emissions in the power generation sector are caused by coal power plants. Converting coal-fired power plants into highly efficient combined cycle plants can reduce CO2 emissions by up to 70%. It also gives you the option to co-fire clean hydrogen in your gas turbine, enabling you to decarbonize your plant operation even further.

Based on the Brownfield Transformation concept, our approach includes repurposing as much of your existing infrastructure as possible to enable a fast transition towards a new energy system while reducing CO₂ emissions at the same time.
Benefits of repowering existing power plants

A full repowering entails not just changing the fuel from coal or oil to gas but converting the steam power plant to a highly efficient combined cycle power plant (CCPP) by reusing infrastructure, site permits and local personnel. Not only is this approach faster and more sustainable but it also saves up to 30% of Capex compared to building a new power plant.
Reusing existing infrastructure for repowering
There are two options to repower your plant: the indoor and the outdoor approach.
bold: the indoor and the outdoor approach.

body.text: With the indoor approach, you can reuse most of the existing infrastructure such as foundations, connections, housing and piping. This saves time and costs. With the outdoor approach, you can start building in parallel when the existing plant is still running to secure critical supplies.

items: Indoor approach
Outdoor approach

body.text: What does it entail?

In principle, a "full repowering" means that one or more gas turbines with downstream heat recovery steam generators replace the old steam generator previously fired with coal or oil. In order to achieve this, various modifications of the steam cycle are necessary, as well as the exchange and retrofit of various components.
What are the prerequisites?

For a full repowering, one needs to make sure that the appropriate gas capacities are available. For the final plan, other factors to be considered are the plant capacity, the heat quantities, and levels to be supplied for district heating and/or process steam applications. Also, one needs to consider the space available, and the condition of the power plant. The overall aim is to keep as much of the existing infrastructure as possible.
What is the effect?

While it is impressive that by converting a conventional coal power plant to a CCPP CO₂ emissions get reduced by up to 70%, it's worth mentioning that this is a result not just from the fuel switch, but also from an increase in the power plant's efficiency from an average of 38% to up to 63%.

items: Boiler Conversion
Topping
Boosting
Parallel Repowering

body.text: Boiler conversion

A boiler conversion involves a modification of the burner technology and a change of coal or oil to gas. While switching to gas as a fuel does not increase the efficiency of the steam plant, it does reduce CO₂ emissions by up to 50%.
Topping

'Topping' requires the installation of a small gas turbine, regardless of whether the fuel is switched from coal to gas or not. The thermal energy contained in the flue gas of the 'topping' gas turbine is fed directly to the steam generator of the existing plant. This results in a slight improvement in overall plant efficiency.
Boosting

Boosting requires the installation of an additional – usually medium – gas turbine and a waste heat boiler. In contrast to topping, the heat energy contained in the flue gas of the gas turbine is used with the aid of a heat exchanger to generate high-pressure steam and to preheat the feed water of the existing process. Boosting makes the steam power plant more flexible, while also increasing efficiency and reducing CO₂ emissions.
Parallel Repowering

Parallel repowering utilizes the steam contained in the flue gas of a newly installed large gas turbine with the aid of a heat recovery steam generator for additional feedwater preheating and steam generation in the existing steam power plant process. This conversion also serves to increase the flexibility and efficiency of steam power plants, but to a greater degree than boosting.
From coal to combined cycle gas plants
Step 1: Design concept

Understanding customer's market environment, the regional energy system and regulatory framework in order to create a customized cost-optimized, efficient, or flexible solution, while aiming at the same time at integrating as many existing assets as possible.
Step 2: Geometrical fit

Analyzing how to integrate the new equipment – such as gas turbines or generators – fit into the existing plant layout and infrastructure. Especially for indoor solutions, it's important to analyze how existing foundations, piping and connections can be reused, while ensuring the new setup will work smoothly and safely.
Step 3: Thermodynamic fit

Identifying the best configuration with the best thermodynamic fit in order to match the future operating regime with the intended business model. This can involve various, far-reaching measures, as, e.g., the steam cycle of a conventional steam power plant differs fundamentally from that of a CCPP.
Step 4: Steam turbine retrofit

Adapting the existing steam turbine and generator to operating parameters of a combined cycle plant. This may concern especially higher temperatures – up to 600°C and more for a steam turbine – that modern CCPPs use today.

items.title: Combined heat and power generation
items.description: Discover Siemens Energy's CHP systems delivering high efficiency, reliable power and heat with up to 93% fuel efficiency for sustainable energy use.
items.tags: Gas turbines;;;Power plants;;;Combined heat and power

body.text: Siemens Energy's combined heat and power (CHP) plants deliver efficient, sustainable energy. Heat production is responsible for 50% of global energy use and 40% of CO₂ emissions, making it the main source of industrial CO₂ output.
What is heat decarbonization?

Heat decarbonization, also known as heat transition, is a process for reducing CO₂ emissions from heat production. As a first step, this can be achieved by making fuel usage more efficient. Later, this fossil fuel can be replaced with carbon-free fuel. Alternatively, heat production can also be electrified by using power from renewable energy. Existing heat networks can be transformed fast and at a large scale into cost-effective and flexible low-carbon energy systems.
What technologies can help to decarbonize heating?

There are several applications that can help to decarbonize heat networks. Siemens Energy offers tailor-made CHP and Power to Heat (P2H) solutions for the residential, commercial and industrial sectors.

CHP generates electricity and heat from a single fuel source. Traditional heating plants emit varying amounts of CO2 depending on the fuel used. Thus, even a simple fuel switch may reduce CO2 emissions by nearly 50%. Additionally, converting the plant into a GT-powered CHP or a Combined Cycle Power Plant with heat extraction can significantly improve its electrical efficiency. As a result, fuel efficiency can be as high as 90% while using as little fuel as possible.
Find out which gas turbine fits best for your application.
CCPPs

Combined Cycle Power Plants (CCPP) use advanced gas and steam turbines for over 64% efficiency, reduced emissions, and flexible output. The efficient use of fuel results in reduced greenhouse gas emissions. CCPPs can quickly ramp up or down, making them ideal for balancing renewable energy sources.

Clean fuels, such as green hydrogen or biofuels, can drastically lower CO2 emissions and eliminate the need for fossil fuels in gas turbines. This is an effective way to future proof a combined cycle power plant and maximize its life cycle. Find out how much carbon footprint you can reduce by burning green hydrogen in your gas turbine. Calculate your carbon dioxide (CO2) reduction and cost-savings potential on carbon certificates.
Calculate your CO₂ emission reduction potential.
Biomass and BECCS

Another decarbonization path is to transform fossil-fired heat generation by switching to sustainably produced biomass in Combined Heat and Power plants. When adding Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS), biomass- or biofuel-based CHP plants can be further transformed into bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), allowing for negative emissions and energy production at the same time.
What is the best heat decarbonization option for your infrastructure?

For maximum efficiency, it often makes sense to combine different technologies. To make the best choice, there are several factors to consider, such as the required temperature level, dispatchable power needs, green electricity cost, availability of waste heat, and annual heat curve. For instance, if you have a lot of renewable energy, it makes sense to consider Power-to-Heat (P2H).
Heat decarbonization offers multiple advantages
Flexibility

The storage of heat is considerably more economical than the storage of electricity. The integration of Power-to-Heat (P2H) technologies with Combined Heat and Power (CHP) systems contributes to greater stability within the power market. CHP plants are capable of efficient and profitable operation, which supports market stability, lowers emissions, and improves overall energy resilience.

faqs.q: What is Concentrated Solar Power (CSP)?
faqs.a: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) is a renewable energy technology that harnesses sunlight to generate electricity. CSP systems use mirrors or heliostats to concentrate a large area of sunlight onto a small area to produce heat. This heat is then used to generate steam, which drives a steam turbine generator set—the heart of the CSP plant. The steam turbine generator set converts the thermal energy from the steam into mechanical energy, which is then transformed into electrical energy. By efficiently translating solar power into electricity, CSP plants can provide a reliable and sustainable energy source. Siemens Energy steam turbines are operating in more than 80% of all CSP plants, making the company the market leader in steam turbines for CSP applications. This technology not only contributes to reducing greenhouse gas emissions but also plays a vital role in the transition to cleaner energy systems.

faqs.q: How does Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants work?
faqs.a: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) is a renewable energy technology that harnesses sunlight to generate electricity. CSP systems use mirrors or heliostats to concentrate a large area of sunlight onto a small area to produce heat. This heat is then used to generate steam, which drives a steam turbine generator set—the heart of the CSP plant. The steam turbine generator set converts the thermal energy from the steam into mechanical energy, which is then transformed into electrical energy. By efficiently translating solar power into electricity, CSP plants can provide a reliable and sustainable energy source.

faqs.q: How does Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) differ from photovoltaic (PV) solar panels?
faqs.a: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) and photovoltaic (PV) solar panels are both technologies used to harness solar energy, but they operate on different principles and have distinct characteristics: Energy Conversion Method: CSP: CSP systems use mirrors or heliostats to concentrate sunlight onto a small area, generating heat that produces steam to drive a steam turbine generator set. This process converts thermal energy into electricity. PV: PV solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity using semiconductor materials that generate an electric current when exposed to sunlight. Scale and Application: CSP: Typically used in large-scale power plants, CSP systems are best suited for utility-scale applications where there is ample land and sunlight. They can also incorporate thermal energy storage to provide electricity even when the sun is not shining. PV: PV panels can be deployed in a variety of settings, from small residential rooftops to large solar farms. They are more versatile and can be installed in diverse locations, including urban areas. Efficiency and Performance: CSP: CSP systems can achieve higher efficiencies in converting solar energy to electricity, especially in regions with high direct sunlight. However, they are less effective in cloudy or diffuse light conditions. PV: PV panels are generally more efficient in converting sunlight to electricity under a wider range of conditions, including cloudy weather. Infrastructure and Cost: CSP: CSP plants typically require more extensive infrastructure and higher initial capital costs due to the need for large land areas, mirrors, and thermal storage systems. PV: PV systems have lower installation costs and can be scaled easily, making them more accessible for residential and commercial applications. In summary, while both CSP and PV technologies harness solar energy, they differ in their methods of energy conversion, scale of application, efficiency, and infrastructure requirements.

faqs.q: What are the advantages of CSP plants?
faqs.a: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants offer several advantages that make them an attractive option for renewable energy generation: High Efficiency: CSP systems can achieve higher thermal efficiencies compared to photovoltaic systems, especially in areas with high direct sunlight. This allows for more effective conversion of solar energy into electricity. Energy Storage Capability: Many CSP plants can incorporate thermal energy storage systems, enabling them to store heat for later use. This capability allows for electricity generation even when the sun is not shining, providing a more reliable and consistent power supply. Reduced Greenhouse Gas Emissions: By utilizing solar energy, CSP plants significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions compared to fossil fuel-based power generation, contributing to a cleaner environment and helping combat climate change. Scalability: CSP plants can be built at various scales, from small installations to large utility-scale facilities, making them adaptable to different energy needs and geographical locations. Job Creation: The construction and operation of CSP plants create jobs in engineering, manufacturing, and maintenance, contributing to local economies and promoting sustainable development. Complementary to Other Energy Sources: CSP can be integrated with other renewable energy sources and traditional power plants, providing a hybrid approach that enhances overall energy reliability and stability. Long Operational Life: CSP plants typically have long operational lifespans, often exceeding 25 years, which allows for sustained energy production and return on investment over time. These advantages position CSP plants as a viable and effective solution for meeting growing energy demands while promoting sustainability and reducing environmental impact.

faqs.q: What are the main challenges or disadvantages of CSP?
faqs.a: While Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants offer several advantages, they also face some challenges and disadvantages: High Initial Costs: CSP plants typically require significant capital investment for construction and infrastructure, which can be a barrier to development compared to other renewable energy technologies. Land Use Requirements: CSP systems require large areas of land to accommodate mirrors or heliostats, which can lead to land use conflicts, especially in densely populated or ecologically sensitive areas. Dependence on Direct Sunlight: CSP technology is most effective in regions with high direct sunlight and can be less efficient in areas with cloudy or diffuse light conditions. This limits the geographical applicability of CSP plants. Complexity of Technology: The technology involved in CSP systems, including thermal storage and heat transfer fluids, can be complex and may require specialized knowledge for operation and maintenance. Intermittency: Although CSP plants can store thermal energy, they still rely on sunlight for operation. This intermittency can pose challenges for grid integration and reliability, particularly during periods of low solar availability. Environmental Impact: The construction and operation of CSP plants can have environmental impacts, including habitat disruption and changes to local ecosystems, which need to be carefully managed. These challenges highlight the need for careful planning, investment, and technological innovation to maximize the potential of CSP as a sustainable energy solution.

faqs.q: How much electricity can a typical CSP plant generate?
faqs.a: A typical Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plant can generate a range of electricity depending on its size, technology, and location. Most CSP plants have capacities ranging from 10 megawatts (MW) to over 100 MW. For example, a 100 MW CSP plant can produce approximately 300,000 to 400,000 megawatt-hours (MWh) of electricity annually, depending on factors such as solar irradiance, operational efficiency, and the inclusion of thermal energy storage. In optimal conditions, larger CSP plants can achieve even higher outputs, contributing significantly to the energy grid and providing a reliable source of renewable energy. The actual generation will vary based on local climate conditions and the specific design of the CSP system.

faqs.q: How does thermal energy storage work in CSP plants?
faqs.a: Thermal energy storage (TES) in Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants allows for the capture and storage of heat generated during sunlight hours, enabling electricity generation even when the sun is not shining. The process typically involves the following steps: Heat Collection: During the day, CSP systems use mirrors or heliostats to concentrate sunlight onto a receiver, where it heats a heat transfer fluid (HTF), commonly molten salt or water. Heat Transfer: The heated HTF is then circulated to a thermal energy storage system, where it transfers its heat to a storage medium. In many CSP plants, molten salt is used due to its high heat capacity and ability to remain in a liquid state at elevated temperatures. Storage: The thermal energy is stored in the form of sensible heat within the molten salt or other storage mediums. This allows the system to retain heat for several hours or even days, depending on the design and capacity of the storage system. Energy Release: When electricity demand increases or during periods of low sunlight, the stored thermal energy is released. The HTF is circulated back to the steam generator, where it transfers heat to water, producing steam. Electricity Generation: The steam drives a steam turbine generator set, converting the thermal energy back into electricity. This process allows CSP plants to provide a continuous and reliable power supply, even during nighttime or cloudy conditions. By incorporating thermal energy storage, CSP plants enhance their operational flexibility and reliability, making them a valuable component of the renewable energy landscape.

faqs.q: Why is concentrated solar power similar to a power plant that uses fossil fuels?
faqs.a: CSP plants are renewable and produce no direct greenhouse gas emissions during operation, while fossil fuel plants contribute to carbon emissions and environmental pollution. Despite this distinction, from a technical perspective, both power plant types share several similarities: Thermal Energy Generation: Both CSP and fossil fuel power plants generate electricity by producing steam. In CSP plants, sunlight is concentrated to heat a fluid, creating steam, while fossil fuel plants burn coal, natural gas, or oil to produce heat that generates steam. Steam Turbine Technology: Both types of power plants utilize steam turbines to convert thermal energy into mechanical energy. The steam produced in both systems drives a turbine connected to a generator, which produces electricity. Heat Transfer Systems: Both CSP and fossil fuel plants rely on heat transfer systems to move thermal energy. In CSP, heat transfer fluids (like molten salt) are used, while fossil fuel plants typically use water or steam as the heat transfer medium. Infrastructure and Operation: The operational infrastructure, including boilers, turbines, and generators, is conceptually similar in both CSP and fossil fuel plants. Both require significant engineering and maintenance to ensure efficient operation. Grid Integration: Both CSP and fossil fuel power plants are integrated into the electrical grid, providing power to meet demand. They can both contribute to base-load or peak-load generation, depending on the design and operational strategy. These technical similarities highlight how CSP can serve as a cleaner alternative to traditional fossil fuel power generation while still utilizing established technologies for electricity production.

Our steam turbines are engineered to deliver high efficiency, quick response times, and durability, enabling CSP plants to maximize energy output while minimizing downtime. body.text: Concentrated solar thermal power is worldwide becoming a more and more important source for power generation. The reasons for this are obvious: The sun is an inexhaustible source for power production. And it is not only a free fuel source but also a complete emissions-free source. Steam turbine generator sets convert solar energy into electricity. Instrumentation and controlls help to make optimal use of every single sun beam. As a market leader in the field, Siemens Energy equipped more than 70 concetrated solar power (CSP) plants all over the world.
Noor Energy 1, Dubai: Welcome to the CSP resurgence

Dubai's new CSP plant is designed to collect heat from the sun and store it in molten salt or convert it directly into electricity via a steam generator set – an ideal solution for providing round-the-clock renewable electricity in unpredictable conditions. Noor Energy 1, the 950 MW Hybrid Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) and PV plant, is the 4th phase of the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Plant and the largest single -site CSP and single hybrid solar power project in the world.
The right equipment for every concentrated solar power technology

Since the solar boom of the eighties in USA, solar thermal energy has been a proven technology. The most common type of plant is the parabolic trough collector, but alternative technologies are rapidly coming to the fore, such as Linear Fresnel collector plants with flat mirrors and central tower plants with slightly curved mirrors or heliostats.

The basic principle is the same for all three plant technologies: Mirrors concentrate the incident solar radiation onto a receiver where it is converted into heat that is used to produce steam to drive a steam turbine. Heat storage systems like molten salt tanks provide for power supply even during unfavorable weather conditions or at night. They significantly increase the number of full-load operation hours with optimal steam turbine efficiency.
Turbines for all main CSP technologies

With our broad steam turbine portfolio, we offer a range of turbines for different types of solar plants and all power outputs. The turbine technology fits all three common concentrated solar power concepts. We were the first steam turbine supplier to re-enter the CSP market in the 21st century, pioneering commercial solutions in the US and Spain. Today, we are the world market leader in steam turbines for CSP plants, and have more than 20 years of experience with steam turbines for daily cycling.
Parabolic trough technology

Parabolic systems use trough-shaped mirrors to focus sunlight onto an absorber tube (receiver) placed in the trough's focal line. The troughs are designed to track the sun along one axis, predominantly north-south. The receivers contain a heat transfer fluid (e.g. synthetic thermal oil, molten salt) which is heated by the focused sunlight. It is circulated in these tubes and pumped through heat exchangers to produce steam.
The parabolic trough technology is currently the best proven and most used technology, even though the live steam parameters are lower than in solar power tower plants.
Solar power tower

A circular array of flat heliostats (suntracking mirrors) concentrates sunlight on to a central receiver at the top of a tower. A heat transfer medium (water/steam, molten salt or air) in the receiver absorbs the thermal energy and transfers it into the steam cycle to generate superheated steam for the turbine.

The advantage over the parabolic trough or Fresnel collector concept is that the sunlight on the central receiver is focused to a smaller area, and the heat transfer medium does not have to be piped around the large solar field. This means that higher working fluid temperatures in the receiver (up to 1000°C) and better steam parameters are feasible, even supercritical steam is expected.
Typical regimes of operation

The number of concentrated solar power plants has increased tremendously in the past ten years. Today we see many different regimes of operations, each of which poses a different challenge to power generation equipment. The design of each steam turbine is adapted to these challenges.

CSP plants require steam turbines which are optimized for their complex and challenging cycle conditions. Bearing in mind that efficiency and total cost of ownership are key to any investment decision, we incorporate operational experience into extensive R&D and engineering activities to adapt the turbines to the specific requirements of the CSP technology.
Excellent daily start-up solutions

Day and night cycle often requires a large number of starts and fast daily startup capabilities from CSP steam turbines. When focusing on annual power production, the short start-up times of the turbines are of great benefit to the CSP plant owner. Daily cycling and temperature variations require special attention.
Reheat improves efficiency

Reheat solutions improve efficiency and reduce problems with erosion/corrosion and moisture in the LP turbine. Our steam turbines meet all customer requirements for economic installation and operation and provide excellent flexibility for all cycling conditions. The turbines are suitable for higher steam parameters and can be operated in non-reheat, single reheat and double reheat cycles.
Reliable steam turbine technology

Our steam turbines are tailored to the customer requirements and shipped assembled for easy installation at site. This reduces time and manpower in the installation phase. All steam turbines are available with axial or radial exhaust and suitable for air- and water-cooled plants.

We provide optimal instrumentation and controls (I&C) design for CSP & Hybrid-PV plants for achieving the full dispatchability of solar energy power plants. With start-up and shut-down 365 days a year, high demands are placed on your plant even on the sunniest of days. Thanks to our I&C's integration expertise in steam turbine controls, balance-of-plant, and solar fields the plant's performance is optimized and long-term reliability is maintained.

body.text: Get answers: FAQs on CSP power plants
What is Concentrated Solar Power (CSP)?

Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) is a renewable energy technology that harnesses sunlight to generate electricity. CSP systems use mirrors or heliostats to concentrate a large area of sunlight onto a small area to produce heat. This heat is then used to generate steam, which drives a steam turbine generator set—the heart of the CSP plant.

The steam turbine generator set converts the thermal energy from the steam into mechanical energy, which is then transformed into electrical energy. By efficiently translating solar power into electricity, CSP plants can provide a reliable and sustainable energy source. Siemens Energy steam turbines are operating in more than 80% of all CSP plants, making the company the market leader in steam turbines for CSP applications. This technology not only contributes to reducing greenhouse gas emissions but also plays a vital role in the transition to cleaner energy systems.
How does Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants work?

The steam turbine generator set converts the thermal energy from the steam into mechanical energy, which is then transformed into electrical energy. By efficiently translating solar power into electricity, CSP plants can provide a reliable and sustainable energy source.
How does Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) differ from photovoltaic (PV) solar panels?
Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) and photovoltaic (PV) solar panels are both technologies used to harness solar energy, but they operate on different principles and have distinct characteristics:
Energy Conversion Method:

CSP: CSP systems use mirrors or heliostats to concentrate sunlight onto a small area, generating heat that produces steam to drive a steam turbine generator set. This process converts thermal energy into electricity.
PV: PV solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity using semiconductor materials that generate an electric current when exposed to sunlight.
Scale and Application:

CSP: Typically used in large-scale power plants, CSP systems are best suited for utility-scale applications where there is ample land and sunlight. They can also incorporate thermal energy storage to provide electricity even when the sun is not shining.
PV: PV panels can be deployed in a variety of settings, from small residential rooftops to large solar farms. They are more versatile and can be installed in diverse locations, including urban areas.
Efficiency and Performance:

CSP: CSP systems can achieve higher efficiencies in converting solar energy to electricity, especially in regions with high direct sunlight. However, they are less effective in cloudy or diffuse light conditions.
PV: PV panels are generally more efficient in converting sunlight to electricity under a wider range of conditions, including cloudy weather. Infrastructure and Cost:
CSP: CSP plants typically require more extensive infrastructure and higher initial capital costs due to the need for large land areas, mirrors, and thermal storage systems.
PV: PV systems have lower installation costs and can be scaled easily, making them more accessible for residential and commercial applications.
In summary, while both CSP and PV technologies harness solar energy, they differ in their methods of energy conversion, scale of application, efficiency, and infrastructure requirements.
What are the advantages of CSP plants?
Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants offer several advantages that make them an attractive option for renewable energy generation:

High Efficiency: CSP systems can achieve higher thermal efficiencies compared to photovoltaic systems, especially in areas with high direct sunlight. This allows for more effective conversion of solar energy into electricity.

Energy Storage Capability: Many CSP plants can incorporate thermal energy storage systems, enabling them to store heat for later use. This capability allows for electricity generation even when the sun is not shining, providing a more reliable and consistent power supply.

Reduced Greenhouse Gas Emissions: By utilizing solar energy, CSP plants significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions compared to fossil fuel-based power generation, contributing to a cleaner environment and helping combat climate change.
Scalability: CSP plants can be built at various scales, from small installations to large utility-scale facilities, making them adaptable to different energy needs and geographical locations.
Job Creation: The construction and operation of CSP plants create jobs in engineering, manufacturing, and maintenance, contributing to local economies and promoting sustainable development.

Complementary to Other Energy Sources: CSP can be integrated with other renewable energy sources and traditional power plants, providing a hybrid approach that enhances overall energy reliability and stability.
Long Operational Life: CSP plants typically have long operational lifespans, often exceeding 25 years, which allows for sustained energy production and return on investment over time.
These advantages position CSP plants as a viable and effective solution for meeting growing energy demands while promoting sustainability and reducing environmental impact.
What are the main challenges or disadvantages of CSP?
While Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants offer several advantages, they also face some challenges and disadvantages:

High Initial Costs: CSP plants typically require significant capital investment for construction and infrastructure, which can be a barrier to development compared to other renewable energy technologies.

Land Use Requirements: CSP systems require large areas of land to accommodate mirrors or heliostats, which can lead to land use conflicts, especially in densely populated or ecologically sensitive areas.

Dependence on Direct Sunlight: CSP technology is most effective in regions with high direct sunlight and can be less efficient in areas with cloudy or diffuse light conditions. This limits the geographical applicability of CSP plants.

Complexity of Technology: The technology involved in CSP systems, including thermal storage and heat transfer fluids, can be complex and may require specialized knowledge for operation and maintenance.

Intermittency: Although CSP plants can store thermal energy, they still rely on sunlight for operation. This intermittency can pose challenges for grid integration and reliability, particularly during periods of low solar availability.
Environmental Impact: The construction and operation of CSP plants can have environmental impacts, including habitat disruption and changes to local ecosystems, which need to be carefully managed.
These challenges highlight the need for careful planning, investment, and technological innovation to maximize the potential of CSP as a sustainable energy solution.
How much electricity can a typical CSP plant generate?

A typical Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plant can generate a range of electricity depending on its size, technology, and location. Most CSP plants have capacities ranging from 10 megawatts (MW) to over 100 MW.

For example, a 100 MW CSP plant can produce approximately 300,000 to 400,000 megawatt-hours (MWh) of electricity annually, depending on factors such as solar irradiance, operational efficiency, and the inclusion of thermal energy storage.

In optimal conditions, larger CSP plants can achieve even higher outputs, contributing significantly to the energy grid and providing a reliable source of renewable energy. The actual generation will vary based on local climate conditions and the specific design of the CSP system.

Thermal energy storage (TES) in Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants allows for the capture and storage of heat generated during sunlight hours, enabling electricity generation even when the sun is not shining. The process typically involves the following steps:

Heat Transfer: The heated HTF is then circulated to a thermal energy storage system, where it transfers its heat to a storage medium. In many CSP plants, molten salt is used due to its high heat capacity and ability to remain in a liquid state at elevated temperatures.

Storage: The thermal energy is stored in the form of sensible heat within the molten salt or other storage mediums. This allows the system to retain heat for several hours or even days, depending on the design and capacity of the storage system.

Energy Release: When electricity demand increases or during periods of low sunlight, the stored thermal energy is released. The HTF is circulated back to the steam generator, where it transfers heat to water, producing steam.

Electricity Generation: The steam drives a steam turbine generator set, converting the thermal energy back into electricity. This process allows CSP plants to provide a continuous and reliable power supply, even during nighttime or cloudy conditions.
By incorporating thermal energy storage, CSP plants enhance their operational flexibility and reliability, making them a valuable component of the renewable energy landscape.
Why is concentrated solar power similar to a power plant that uses fossil fuels?

CSP plants are renewable and produce no direct greenhouse gas emissions during operation, while fossil fuel plants contribute to carbon emissions and environmental pollution. Despite this distinction, from a technical perspective, both power plant types share several similarities:

Thermal Energy Generation: Both CSP and fossil fuel power plants generate electricity by producing steam. In CSP plants, sunlight is concentrated to heat a fluid, creating steam, while fossil fuel plants burn coal, natural gas, or oil to produce heat that generates steam.

Steam Turbine Technology: Both types of power plants utilize steam turbines to convert thermal energy into mechanical energy. The steam produced in both systems drives a turbine connected to a generator, which produces electricity.

Heat Transfer Systems: Both CSP and fossil fuel plants rely on heat transfer systems to move thermal energy. In CSP, heat transfer fluids (like molten salt) are used, while fossil fuel plants typically use water or steam as the heat transfer medium.

Infrastructure and Operation: The operational infrastructure, including boilers, turbines, and generators, is conceptually similar in both CSP and fossil fuel plants. Both require significant engineering and maintenance to ensure efficient operation.

Grid Integration: Both CSP and fossil fuel power plants are integrated into the electrical grid, providing power to meet demand. They can both contribute to base-load or peak-load generation, depending on the design and operational strategy.

These technical similarities highlight how CSP can serve as a cleaner alternative to traditional fossil fuel power generation while still utilizing established technologies for electricity production.

Increasing transparency in environmental footprint assessments
